candidates.title: Structural and Functional Characterization of Cysteate Fatty Acyltransferases Involved in Bacterial Sulfonolipid Biosynthesis
candidates.authors: Pang C, Liu M, Gu Y, Zhou J, Tang X.
candidates.abstract: AbstractSulfonolipids are bacterial sphingolipid-like lipids featuring a sulfonated long-chain base derived from cysteate. Although several cysteate-utilizing enzymes have been implicated in sulfonolipid biosynthesis, their phylogenetic relationships and the structural basis of cysteate utilization remain poorly understood. Here, we combined phylogenetic analysis, biochemical characterization, X-ray crystallography, and mutagenesis to investigate cysteate fatty acyltransferase (CFAT) homologues involved in bacterial sulfonolipid biosynthesis. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that previously characterized cysteate-utilizing enzymes form a distinct branch within the broader serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT)-related pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme superfamily. Biochemical assay on six representatives confirmed a conserved cysteate-dependent long-chain-base synthase activity and a strong preference for cysteate over serine, glycine, and alanine. To elucidate this specificity, we solved crystal structures of a representative CFAT from Capnocytophaga ochracea in both PLP-bound and PLP–cysteate-bound states, capturing a PLP–cysteate external aldimine intermediate. This structure reveals a composite active-site pocket formed across the dimer interface, where the conserved PLP-dependent catalytic scaffold is retained but the substrate-binding pocket is significantly remodeled compared to canonical SPTs. Structure-guided mutagenesis identified key residues important for cysteate-dependent catalysis but failed to generate serine activity. Together, these findings establish CFAT homologues as a functionally coherent family of cysteate-utilizing enzymes and provide critical molecular insights into bacterial sulfonolipid biosynthesis.Keywords: sulfonolipid biosynthesis, PLP-dependent enzyme, serine palmitoyltransferase, cysteate fatty acyltransferase (CFAT), structure biology

candidates.title: Reversible autoinhibition of the bacterial replication-licensing Hda–β clamp complex
candidates.abstract: AbstractBacterial DNA replication must be tightly controlled to ensure once-per-cell-cycle initiation, requiring precise regulation of the initiator DnaA. The conserved RIDA pathway inactivates DnaA through the Hda–β sliding clamp (DnaN) complex, yet how this system is dynamically regulated has remained unclear. Here, we show that the Hda–DnaN complex exists as a concentration-dependent oligomeric ensemble rather than a static assembly. Using cryo-electron microscopy and mass photometry, we resolve multiple structural states, including an autoinhibited hetero-octamer, a hetero-hexamer intermediate, and a RIDA-compatible hetero-trimer. Structural comparison of these states suggests a plausible route of oligomeric interconversion involving progressive destabilization of Hda self-association, accompanied by exposure of the catalytic arginine finger required for DnaA inactivation. We further propose that this equilibrium operates as a titration-like mechanism that converts local protein concentration into functional states. Together, our findings establish reversible oligomerization as a potential regulatory principle for bacterial replication licensing.

candidates.title: Catalysis tuned for metabolic sensing: dynamics and mechanism of the RNA methyltransferase METTL16
candidates.authors: Stamm F, Wan Z, Vargas-Rosales P, Corbeski I, Braud E, Iannazzo L, Cui Q, Caflisch A.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe methyltransferase-like protein 16 (METTL16) is the writer enzyme that methylates adenosine to form N6-methyladenosine (m6A) on U6 spliceosomal RNA and MAT2A mRNA. The latter encodes the enzyme responsible for the synthesis of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM). Since methylation influences the stability of MAT2A mRNA, METTL16 is the sensor of SAM in the cell. Here, we investigate the (co)substrate recognition and catalytic mechanism of METTL16 by a combination of in vitro and simulation methods. We first solved the crystal structures of METTL16 in complex with bisubstrate analogs (BAs), conjugates of a SAM-like moiety connected to the N6-atom of adenosine. The METTL16/BA crystal structures provide an atomistic picture of a transition-state mimic of methyl transfer. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations started from complexes with oligonucleotide-RNA modeled on the METTL16/BAs structures show rapid unbinding of SAM. The presence of the MAT2A hairpin 1 RNA stabilizes SAM in its recognition pocket, and substantially reduces the intrinsic flexibility of the R-loop and N-terminal segment of METTL16. Quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) free energy calculations provide evidence that methyl transfer occurs without prior deprotonation of adenosine-N6. Furthermore, the simulations indicate that electrostatic interactions between the charged groups of SAM and the catalytic pocket are less pronounced for METTL16 than for METTL3–14, which is the main m6A-RNA writer enzyme. The multidisciplinary approach used here sheds light on the intrinsic plasticity of METTL16, the rigidification upon RNA-substrate binding, the catalytic mechanism, and (co)product release. Overall, our study suggests that the latter step is rate-limiting.

candidates.title: A novel double-mAb sandwich ELISA utilizing broad-spectrum neutralizing antibodies as an in vitro alternative to the rabies vaccine NIH potency assay
candidates.authors: Cai M, Wu X, Shi L, Tong J, He C, Nie J, Yang Y, Ren J, Li Y, Mao Q, Wang Y, Cao S, Huang W.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackgroundRabies remains a devastating zoonotic disease, with prevention measures relying heavily on post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Evaluating rabies vaccine potency traditionally relies on the in vivo National Institutes of Health (NIH) mouse challenge assay, which is limited by long testing cycles, low reproducibility, and high animal consumption. Developing broad-spectrum monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and alternative in vitro assays is essential to advance rabies prevention and improve vaccine quality control.MethodsIn this study, we characterized three human-mouse chimeric mAbs (05-2F10, 06-2A12, and 07-4D8-1C1) with broad-spectrum neutralizing activity. Leveraging in vitro pseudovirus neutralization assays, we evaluated candidate mAbs for high neutralizing capacity and low sensitivity to variation to select optimal pairs for assay development. Using these selected mAbs, a double-antibody sandwich ELISA was established to quantify glycoprotein (G) antigen content in human rabies vaccines.ResultsThe three chimeric mAbs exhibited exceptional in vitro neutralization potency and breadth. The established double-antibody sandwich ELISA successfully quantified G antigen content in human rabies vaccines. Importantly, a high correlation was demonstrated between the antigen content quantified by this ELISA and the potency data generated via the traditional in vivo NIH mouse challenge test.ConclusionCollectively, these findings provide a robust technical framework for replacing the traditional NIH potency assay with a reliable in vitro method, fully aligning with the 3Rs principles of animal welfare.Keywords: ELISA, in vitro alternative method, monoclonal antibodies, pseudovirus neutralization, rabies virus

candidates.title: Identification of small-molecule inhibitors of the immune system repressor Regnase-1
candidates.authors: Millius A, Yew CT, Misumi Y, Yu J, Takaya D, Miyakawa S, Choi ES, Lee HJ, Andini TM, Khalaf F, Maeda K, Fukuzawa K, Kurisu G, Akira S, Park S, Standley DM.
candidates.abstract: AbstractRegnase-1 is an essential RNase that suppresses immune cell activation by targeting the mRNA of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin 6 (IL-6). Although genetic inhibition of Regnase-1 activity in CD8+ T cells has been shown to enhance antitumor immunity, no molecular inhibitors of Regnase-1 have been reported. By exploiting a library of nucleic acid analogs in conjunction with an RNA displacement assay, we identified multiple candidate competitors of Regnase-1 RNA substrates. Among these, suramin—an approved drug for treating African sleeping sickness—and several of its derivatives displaced Regnase-1 RNA targets with submicromolar affinity, competitively inhibited Regnase-1–mediated degradation of RNA in vitro, and enhanced Il6 mRNA levels and IL-6 production in mouse embryonic fibroblasts. A 2.62 Å crystal structure revealed that suramin bound to the Regnase-1 active site, coordinating with the catalytic Mg2+. Quantum chemical calculations further elucidated qualitative interactions between suramin and surrounding residues of Regnase-1. These findings establish suramin as a small-molecule inhibitor of Regnase-1–mediated RNA decay.

candidates.title: Insights into pyrazinone biosynthesis from biochemical and cryo-EM studies of the hybrid NRPS-PKS enzyme CorA
candidates.authors: Yang Q, Wang Q, Li X, Sang M, Hu T, Wang D, Zhu L, Wu D, Li Y, Li S, Wu C, Zhang H, Zhang W.
candidates.abstract: Hybrid nonribosomal peptide synthetase-polyketide synthase (NRPS-PKS) systems integrate peptide and polyketide biosynthetic logic to assemble complex natural products. CorA, a prototypical NRPS-PKS hybrid from the myxobacterium Corallococcus exiguus SDU70, is responsible for producing 5-alkylated pyrazinones, a family of bioactive metabolites with morphogenetic roles in myxobacterial development. Previous studies have identified CorA as a core biosynthetic enzyme responsible for the formation of 5-methylated pyrazinones; however, the structural and mechanistic basis underlying its capacity to recognize diverse dipeptide substrates and accommodate distinct acyl-CoA extender units remains elusive. Here, combining in vitro biochemistry, structure determination by cryo-electron microscopy (EM), mutagenesis, and molecular docking, we show that full-length CorA generates twelve distinct 5-alkylated pyrazinone products using six amino acid combinations and two acyl-CoA extenders, highlighting an unusually permissive gating mechanism within the KS domain. The 3.1-Å cryo-EM structure of the CorA KS-AT didomain provides structural insights into its substrate-binding architecture. The atypical SGFH motif of the AT domain permits dual binding of M-CoA and MM-CoA, and an irregular non-helical loop in the KS domain creates an open pocket for large amino acid-derived intermediates. These distinctive architectural features confer robust substrate promiscuity on CorA. Collectively, our structural data offers insights to understand the wide substrate compatibility of NRPS-PKS hybrid enzymes and may offer useful clues for the rational engineering of biosynthetic pathways to diversify natural product scaffolds.

candidates.title: A recyclable [DABCO][Imi]2 deep eutectic solvent for multicomponent synthesis of 1,2-dihydropyridine-3-carbonitriles: in vitro antiproliferative and in silico molecular evaluation
candidates.authors: Pham T, Tran T, Tran D, Nguyen H, Nguyen H.
candidates.abstract: This study reports the synthesis of a novel deep eutectic solvent (DES), [DABCO][Imi]2, for the multicomponent synthesis of 2-oxo-4,6-disubstituted-1,2-dihydropyridine-3-carbonitrile derivatives. A novel DES was successfully synthesized and structurally characterized using 1H NMR, 13C NMR, FT-IR spectroscopy, and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). A series of 30 derivatives was synthesized in moderate isolated yields (up to 40%). The synthesized compounds were evaluated for their inhibitory activity against human melanoma A375 cancer cells. Among the synthesized compounds, (5cg) and (5ch) exhibited the highest antiproliferative activity against A375 cells, with IC50 values of 17.44 ± 0.09 mM and 12.04 ± 0.12 mM, respectively. Molecular docking suggested that SIRT1 may serve as a potential molecular target for these compounds. Molecular docking and ADME prediction suggested that these compounds possess acceptable drug-like properties and may serve as suitable starting points for further structural optimization.

candidates.title: Acarbose differentially affects gut microbial metabolism of maltose and sucrose, distinctly modulating host metabolism
candidates.authors: Yoshikawa H, Lee E, Hatano R, Taki Y, Takaya A, Eguchi A, Goto Y, Miyamoto J, Kimura I, Tanaka T, Miki T.
candidates.abstract: SummaryGut microbiota act as beneficial symbionts of the hosts. Administration of α-glucosidase inhibitors (α-GIs) is considered to promote the microbiota’s carbohydrate availability, modulating short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. However, it remains unclear whether host-microbiota interaction differs depending on α-GI types (e.g., acarbose versus miglitol) and carbohydrate types co-administered. In this study, we demonstrate that acarbose is transported through bacterial outer membrane porins, LamB and ScrY, and inhibits maltose metabolism in Escherichia coli. Furthermore, studies using Klebsiella pneumoniae reveal that acarbose suppresses utilization of maltose, but not that of sucrose. When co-administered with acarbose in mice, sucrose, relative to maltose, enhances SCFA production, suppresses glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) secretion, and protects against high-fat diet-induced obesity, underscoring the importance of sucrose as a microbiota-dependent beneficial factor, but not a culprit in host metabolism. In conclusion, acarbose regulates host metabolic processes partly by modulating gut microbial metabolism in a carbohydrate-type-dependent manner.

candidates.title: Amino Acids in the RSSY Motif of Lipoyl Synthase Control Substrate Binding and Reactivity
candidates.authors: Jeyachandran V, Lanz N, Pandelia M, Rectenwald J, Pendyala J, Maurya R, Boal A, Krebs C, Booker S.
candidates.abstract: The last step in the biosynthesis of the lipoyl cofactor (LipCo) is the addition of two sulfur atoms at C6 and C8 of an n-octanoyl chain attached by an amide linkage to a target lysyl residue of a lipoyl carrier protein. This reaction is catalyzed by lipoyl synthase, a member of the radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) superfamily. Lipoyl synthase requires two [4Fe-4S] clusters. One cluster is used to cleave SAM reductively to generate two 5′-deoxyadenosyl 5′-radicals (5′-dA•), which abstract the C6 and C8 hydrogen atoms (H•) of the substrate in two sequential steps. The second cluster, termed the auxiliary cluster, is consumed during turnover to provide the attached sulfur atoms. The auxiliary cluster is ligated by three cysteines in a CX4CX5C motif and one serine residue (Ser308 in Escherichia coli) in a highly conserved R306SS308Y motif in the C-terminal region of the protein. Here, we show that Arg306 and Ser308 are absolutely required for LipCo formation. Substitution of Arg306 with Lys results in an essentially inactive protein due to poor substrate binding and positioning in the active site. Multiple substitutions of Ser308 were engineered. Most notably, the S308C and S308A variants greatly diminished LipCo formation. However, the S308C variant resulted in greater production of the 6-mercaptooctanoyl intermediate and the formation of a desaturated product, identified as a 6-octenoyl group. Furthermore, the 3Fe cluster formed during degradation of the auxiliary cluster in the course of C6 sulfur substitution in the wild-type reaction is not observed with the S308C variant. Instead, the auxiliary cluster remains tetranuclear and forms a monothiolated cross-linked species with a high-spin, S = 7/2 configuration that decays to the 6-octenoyl-containing product. Other amino acids in the RSSY motif were not essential for catalysis.

candidates.title: An Oral Antiviral Combination Against Severe COVID‐19 Enabled by the Synergistic Mechanisms of Action of Auranofin and Remdesivir
candidates.authors: Khatun O, Narayan R, Nagaraj S, Shiraz R, Kaliappan A, Kaur S, Singh A, Shanmugam Selvaraj S, Rudramurthy G, Naveenkumar C, Narayanan S, Shandil R, Tomar S, Tripathi S.
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTAuranofin, an FDA‐approved oral anti‐rheumatic drug, was previously shown by our group to restrict Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus‐2 (SARS‐CoV‐2) replication and pathology in preclinical models. Here, we systematically characterized its mechanism of action (MOA) through biochemical drug‐protein interactions, cell‐based mechanistic assays, and preclinical efficacy studies. Auranofin directly binds and inhibits SARS‐CoV‐2 MPro while simultaneously targeting multiple stages of the viral life cycle, disrupting endosomal trafficking, suppressing Spike S1/S2 proteolytic processing, impairing syncytia formation, and attenuating NF‐κB‐driven proinflammatory signaling. In cell culture, Auranofin demonstrated robust synergy with Remdesivir but competed with the MPro inhibitor Nirmatrelvir, informing rational combination design. In mice infected with the SARS‐CoV‐2 Delta variant, the oral combination of Auranofin and the Remdesivir prodrug GS‐621763 outperformed monotherapy, markedly reducing viral replication, inflammatory cytokine responses, and lung pathology, and improving clinical outcomes. These findings establish a multi‐target antiviral MOA of Auranofin and provide a mechanistic rationale for an all‐oral antiviral combination regimen against COVID‐19.

candidates.title: Antibacterial Activity of Equisetin from Endophytic Fusarium incarnatum JMB4 Associated with Jatropha multifida L. Against MRSA: Experimental and In Silico Insights
candidates.authors: Satriawan H, Khalda R, Li H, Setiawansyah A, Kuo P, Handayani D.
candidates.abstract: AbstractAn antibacterial metabolite was isolated from the endophytic fungus Fusarium incarnatum JMB4 associated with Jatropha multifida L. by bioactivity-guided chromatography and recrystallization. The isolated compound was assigned as equisetin using UV–vis, FTIR, LC–MS/MS, and 1H NMR data. Anti-MRSA activity was evaluated by disk diffusion, with chloramphenicol and amoxicillin as antibiotic comparators. At 1% (w/v; 100 μg/disk), equisetin produced an inhibition zone of 23.94 ± 0.66 mm; the recorded comparator zones were 24.71 ± 0.68 mm for chloramphenicol (30 μg/disk) and 11.76 ± 0.66 mm for amoxicillin (25 μg/disk). The lowest tested equisetin concentration producing a measurable zone was 78.1 μg/mL (7.03 ± 0.25 mm). This diffusion end point does not represent a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), and the unequal disk loads preclude a direct comparison of intrinsic antibacterial potency. Exploratory docking against penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a) yielded a score of −5.5041 kcal/mol and a predicted pose outside the canonical catalytic pocket. A 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation described the behavior of the modeled complex but did not establish PBP2a inhibition. These results document anti-MRSA activity of the isolated compound under the tested conditions; standardized MIC determination and further structural validation remain necessary.

candidates.authors: Hasan M, Ahmed M, Saha N, Ahmmed R, Talukder M, Shahir N, Rafi N, Pervin F, Khan M, Karim M, Islam M.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThis study evaluated the antineoplastic potential of L. rubiginosa leaves by integrating phytochemical, antioxidant, in vivo, and in silico approaches. The methanolic extract of L. rubiginosa leaves (LRLME) contained high levels of phenolics (61.292 ± 0.902 mg GAE/g) and flavonoids (130.718 1.862 mg CAE/g) and exhibited strong antioxidant activity in the total antioxidant capacity, DPPH, and ABTS assays. Cytotoxicity assessment using the brine shrimp lethality assay indicated low toxicity, with an LC50 of 661.278 μg/mL. In vivo antitumor studies revealed that intraperitoneal administration of LRLME (40 mg/kg) significantly inhibited Ehrlich Ascites Carcinoma (EAC) cell proliferation by 54.31% (p < 0.001) and extended the lifespan of mice implanted with tumors by 97.30% (p < 0.001). Treatment with LRLME also significantly restored hematological parameters, including red and white blood cell counts and hemoglobin levels, toward normal values compared with untreated controls. Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) profiling revealed 54 phytochemical constituents, which were thereafter screened through molecular docking, ADMET profiling, and molecular dynamics simulations targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). Three compounds, namely (−)-norephedrine, cathine, and phenylephrine, demonstrated the highest binding affinities (−6.644, −6.474, and −6.000 kcal/mol, respectively) and favorable pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles. Molecular dynamics studies further affirmed the sustained stable interactions and conformational stability of these compounds within the EGFR active site. Collectively, these findings suggest that L. rubiginosa exhibits significant anticancer activity against EAC cells and may serve as a potential natural reservoir of EGFR inhibitors for future therapeutic development.Keywords: Lepisanthes rubiginosa, Phytopharmaceutical potential, Antioxidant activity, Antineoplastic activity, Molecular docking, MD simulations

candidates.title: Astragaloside IV attenuates ferroptosis-related testicular injury in rats with experimental varicocele
candidates.authors: Gao B, Liu S, Sun M, Chen W, Shi Z, Gao J, Zhong C.
candidates.abstract: Varicocele is an important correctable cause of male infertility. Oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation contribute to the associated testicular injury, but the role of ferroptosis remains controversial. Astragaloside IV (AS-IV), a quality-control metabolite of Astragali radix, has antioxidant activity and can modulate ferroptosis-related processes, yet its effect in varicocele is unclear. This study evaluated whether AS-IV attenuates testicular injury in experimental varicocele and examined ferroptosis-related mechanisms. A Sprague–Dawley rat model was established by partial ligation of the left renal vein and treated with oral AS-IV; Ferrostatin-1 served as a pharmacological comparator. Label-free proteomics, histopathology, biochemical assays and targeted molecular analyses were combined with a TM4 Sertoli-cell model of RSL3-induced injury. AS-IV lessened tubular injury and improved Johnsen scores in a dose-related manner, reduced testicular Fe2+, ROS and MDA, and raised the GSH/GSSG ratio. Proteomics showed partial reversal of lipid-metabolism and ferroptosis-related enrichment after AS-IV. These changes were accompanied by recovery of androgen receptor (AR) and MBOAT2. In TM4 cells, AS-IV improved viability and lowered C11-BODIPY oxidation after RSL3; enzalutamide weakened the effects of AS-IV on lipid peroxidation and MBOAT2 and only partly reduced the viability rescue. The findings provide experimental evidence that AS-IV ameliorates varicocele-related testicular injury and that AR/MBOAT2-related signalling may participate.

candidates.title: Carbothioamide functionalized paroxetine analogues as antiparasitic agents targeting the hypoxanthine-guanine-xanthine phosphoribosyltransferase enzyme: Synthesis, characterization, biochemical, biophysical, and in silico studies
candidates.authors: Hammal L, Ali M, Zafar N, Mari SH, Zafar H, Wahab AT, Siddiqui H, Javaid S, Choudhary MI.
candidates.abstract: AbstractHypoxanthine guanine xanthine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGXPRT) is one of the central enzymes of purine salvage pathway of protozoan parasites, including Plasmodium. These parasites are purine auxotrophs, and rely on purine salvage pathway for nucleic acid synthesis. Inhibiting the enzymatic activity can effectively reduce the parasite- induced infections, including malaria. In this context, a library of new carbothioamide derivatives 1–17 of paroxetine was synthesized via single-step chemical transformation strategy with a series of substituted phenyl isothiocyanates. All compounds were purified, and their structures were deduced by using spectroscopic techniques, such as mass, FT-IR, UV, and 1H-, and 13C-NMR. These compounds were evaluated for their HGXPRT inhibitory activity via in vitro UV-based spectrophotometric assay. All derivatives 1–17 showed varying potential to inhibit the enzyme activity with IC50 values between 19.0 to 76.9 µM, with highest activity showed by compound 13 (IC50 = 19.0 ± 2.09 µM) within the series, but remained less potent than the standard (9-deazaguanine, IC50 = 12.00 ± 1.0 µM). Biophysical, molecular docking, and molecular simulation studies were carried out further to analyse the enzyme-inhibitor interaction, and stability. These compounds were predicted to occupy the putative allosteric site of enzyme. Furthermore, cytotoxic profile of these compounds were also evaluated via ADMET analysis and MTT assay, and found to be largely non-cytotoxic. The current study has identified potential hits against HGXPRT enzyme that could further be investigated as anti-parasitic drugs.

candidates.authors: Barbosa Bento P, Almeida D, Ciancaglini I, Roman E, Muniz J, Albino dos Reis R, Squina F, Garcia W.
candidates.abstract: AbstractEsterases are a class of enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of carboxylic ester bonds and are widely utilized in the food, pharmaceutical, and detergent industries. In this study, we report the identification and comprehensive characterization of a novel esterase (TbEst) from the Thermotogaceae family, a group of thermophilic bacteria. The predicted three-dimensional structure of TbEst displays a classical α/β-hydrolase fold with a conserved Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad. TbEst was cloned, heterologously expressed, and purified via a multistep chromatographic protocol. The melting temperature of TbEst at pH 8.0 was 78 °C, confirming its thermostability. Furthermore, TbEst exhibited activity against p-nitrophenyl acetate, confirming its esterase activity, with optimal performance at pH 8.0 and 50 °C. Notably, TbEst exhibited catalytic activity toward broad aromatic and aliphatic esters, reinforcing its versatility for diverse biotechnological applications. Furthermore, the present study describes the successful nanoscale immobilization of TbEst onto Ag/AgCl nanoparticles (TbEst@Ag/AgCl-NPs) via a facile photochemical route. TbEst@Ag/AgCl-NPs were highly stable, with different geometries including spherical and cubic; it was crystalline in nature, and had a mean diameter of 100 nm. Notably, TbEst retained its catalytic activity upon nanoscale immobilization onto Ag/AgCl-NPs. Furthermore, nanoscale immobilization conferred enhanced thermostability and significantly prolonged the active lifetime of the bioconjugate compared to the free enzyme. The data described here should provide a useful basis for future research and biotechnological applications of esterases and nanoimmobilized esterases.

candidates.title: Complex post-translational regulation of the plant shikimate pathway
candidates.authors: Pascual M, Rivas E, Castro-Rodriguez V, Ginés A, El-Azaz J, de la Torre F.
candidates.abstract: AbstractPost-translational modifications (PTMs) are crucial regulators of protein function, influencing most cellular processes in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. The fundamental effect of PTMs on metabolic control has been reported for most metabolic pathways in organisms ranging from animals and plants to bacteria and fungi. However, the impact of PTMs on the regulation of the plant shikimate pathway, which connects central carbon metabolism with the synthesis of aromatic amino acids and represents one of the largest metabolic fluxes on Earth, remains largely unexplored. In this study, we address the identification of PTMs affecting the enzymes of the shikimate pathway in Arabidopsis thaliana. Following a strategy based on transient expression in protoplasts, immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometric analysis, we have identified a large and varied collection of PTMs affecting the 20 alternative isoenzymes involved in the shikimate and phenylalanine (Phe) biosynthesis pathways. Our analysis revealed glycosylation, phosphorylation, methylation, nitration, and acetylation as the predominant modifications. Notably, we have identified multiple phosphorylation events that expand those previously reported. Additionally, we characterized two phosphorylation events affecting chorismate mutase 1 (AtCM1), the committed enzyme in the phenylalanine/tyrosine biosynthetic pathway. Enzymatic assays using phosphomimic recombinant pure AtCM1 support that these PTMs significantly modulate the enzyme´s allosteric behaviour, highlighting its PTMs role in fine-tuning metabolic regulation. Furthermore, functional characterization of prephenate aminotransferase (PAT) showed that phosphomimetic substitutions at Ser240 and Ser247 abolished enzymatic activity, supporting a regulatory role for phosphorylation in aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. Overall, the identification of these PTMs provides new insights into the regulation of metabolic flux through the shikimate and Phe biosynthetic pathways.Keywords: Arabidopsis, aromatic amino acids, chloroplast, chorismate mutase, plant metabolism, post-translational modification, prephenate aminotransferase

candidates.title: Conserved IQ motifs, divergent apo‐calmodulin recognition in UBE3B and UBE3C
candidates.journal: Protein Science : A Publication of the Protein Society
candidates.authors: Schaffter E, Lu X, Tinklenberg A, Hill M, Levin R, Tabima J, Huo S, Spratt D.
candidates.abstract: AbstractCalmodulin (CaM) regulates diverse signaling proteins through recognition of short linear motifs, including isoleucine‐glutamine (IQ) motifs that commonly bind Ca2+‐free CaM (apo‐CaM). The homologous to E6AP carboxyl terminus (HECT) E3 ubiquitin ligases ubiquitin protein ligase E3B (UBE3B) and ubiquitin protein ligase E3C (UBE3C) are closely related enzymes that both contain N‐terminal IQ motifs, yet whether these motifs encode conserved modes of apo‐CaM recognition has remained unclear. Here, we combined isothermal titration calorimetry, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and computational modeling to compare apo‐CaM binding by the UBE3B and UBE3C IQ motifs. The UBE3B IQ motif bound apo‐CaM with high affinity and preferentially engaged the CaM C‐lobe, whereas the UBE3C IQ motif interacted more weakly under the same conditions. NMR titrations revealed distinct molecular recognition modes—UBE3B IQ binding occurred in slow exchange and produced a localized C‐lobe interaction surface, while UBE3C IQ binding occurred in fast exchange and generated smaller, more distributed chemical shift perturbations. Structural models and molecular dynamics simulations provide a framework for interpreting these divergent apo‐CaM engagement modes despite conservation of canonical IQ motif features. Phylogenetic analysis further suggests that the UBE3B and UBE3C IQ motifs have followed divergent evolutionary trajectories within the broader IQ motif family. Together, these findings show that conserved IQ motifs in related HECT ligases can encode different apo‐CaM binding modes, providing a molecular basis for divergent CaM‐mediated regulation of UBE3B and UBE3C.

candidates.title: Design, synthesis, and in vitro antiproliferative evaluation of dasatinib/HO-1 inhibitor codrugs towards glioblastoma therapy
candidates.authors: Pittalà V, Salerno L, Consoli V, D'Amico AG, Sorrenti V, Vanella L, Centamore G, Terlati C, Mocka S, Modica MN, Romeo G, Schiano ME, Sodano F, Helal MA, Intagliata S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractHerein, dasatinib (DASA) and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) inhibitor codrugs were designed and synthesized. Derivatization of DASA was performed by preserving the structural features essential for target inhibition and was rationally guided by molecular modelling studies. Two out of three synthesized codrugs showed the ability to inhibit HO-1 activity in a low micromolar range (i.e., 2.12 and 1.00 μM for TC7 and TC8, respectively), while all derivatives retained a significant capability of inhibiting the cSRC tyrosine kinase with sub-micromolar potency (i.e., 0.0023–0.0255 μM). Of note, derivative TC7 exhibited significant in vitro antiproliferative activity against U87MG glioblastoma cells, likely mediated by HO inhibition and accompanied by a ∼1.5-fold increase in intracellular ROS levels compared with the control. Also, assessment of the most promising codrug, TC7, revealed high chemical and enzymatic stability (t1/2 >24 h). While additional optimization will be required to further improve its drug-like profile, TC7 emerged as the most promising compound evaluated in this study and represents a suitable starting point for future development. Collectively, these results serve as a proof of concept supporting a potential new codrugs strategy combining HO-1 and cSRC inhibition for glioblastoma therapy.

candidates.title: Dioscin Promotes Ferroptosis in Cervical Cancer Cells via the TIGAR‐ROS Axis
candidates.authors: Liu Y, Xi H, Min S, Yang H, Hou L, Zhang H, Tan Y.
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTCervical cancer seriously threatens women's life and health, highlighting the urgent need for targeted therapies. TP53‐induced glycolysis regulatory phosphatase (TIGAR), upregulated in cervical cancer and regulated by HPV E6, may be involved in cervical cancer progression, making its inhibition a potential therapeutic strategy. This study aims to investigate the role and mechanism of TIGAR in cervical cancer ferroptosis resistance and identify a TIGAR‐targeting drug to suppress cervical cancer advancement. Through RNA‐seq, transmission electron microscopy, and western blotting, we found that TIGAR knockdown significantly promoted ferroptosis by increasing intracellular lipid reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. Furthermore, through molecular docking, CETSA, and SPR analysis, we identified Dioscin as a compound that binds to TIGAR. Dioscin treatment effectively inhibited cervical tumors via TIGAR both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, Dioscin interacted with TIGAR and promoted ferroptosis, at least in part, through the TIGAR–ROS axis. Collectively, these findings indicate that TIGAR suppresses ferroptosis via lipid ROS reduction, while Dioscin counteracts this process, at least in part, through the TIGAR–ROS axis. Thus, Dioscin holds promise as a potential targeted therapeutic agent for cervical cancer.Keywords: cervical cancer, dioscin, ferroptosis, ROS, TIGAR

candidates.title: Dynamics of the Myoglobin/Heme Complex: A Limited Proteolysis Perspective
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe dynamics and stabilities (i.e., physicochemical properties) of proteins and protein complexes are dictated by the solution environment. Changes in the solution environment may alter the distribution of states present in solution (i.e., the free-energy landscape) and thus their physicochemical properties. This work examines the effects of temperature (4 °C, 21 °C, and 37 °C), electrospray ionization buffers (ammonium acetate (AmAc) and triethylammonium acetate (TEAA)), and solvent (H2O and D2O) on the physicochemical characteristics of the myoglobin/heme complex using limited proteolysis (i.e., trypsin digestion) and ion mobility-mass spectrometry (IM-MS). Electrospray ionization mass spectra of peptides formed by limited proteolysis showed increased peptide abundances at higher temperatures and in the absence of buffer molecules relative to the intact precursors. Interestingly, peptide abundances in D2O are more consistent across the temperature range studied relative to the peptide abundances in H2O, which demonstrates that D2O not only stabilizes proteins but acts as a kinetic trap for specific protein conformations. As an example, buffer components and D2O stabilize the myoglobin/heme interaction, as is evidenced by the modulation of peptide 64–77, an α-helical region that interacts with heme, and by shifts in the abundances of unfolded protein precursors. Lastly, IM-MS analysis of digested peptides suggests that AmAc alters the tertiary structure of the myoglobin/heme complex, whereas TEAA alters the secondary structure of the complex. The preservation of secondary structure in TEAA is further illustrated by the shift in arrival time distributions of 1+ ions in TEAA relative to the 2+, 3+, 4+, and 5+ ions present in other buffer conditions. Overall, the data show that buffer-solvent interactions govern the hydration of myoglobin and consequently, the physicochemical properties of the complex.Keywords: limited proteolysis, mass spectrometry, ion mobility, average charge state, hydration, buffer molecules

candidates.title: Evaluation of carvacrol and quercetin against surgical site infection pathogen Escherichia coli: In silico target identification, anti-biofilm efficacy, and cellular safety
candidates.authors: Kanungo A, Kumar R, Acharya S.
candidates.abstract: Surgical site infections (SSIs) are postoperative complications driven by biofilm development on surgical wounds or implanted medical equipment. SSIs create a risk in terms of morbidity, extended hospitalization, and in extreme cases may cause mortality. The multi-drug-resistant bacteria, which frequently exist as poly-microbial communities in biofilms, present multiple tolerance mechanisms that render SSIs extremely difficult to treat with standard antibiotics. Besides, biofilm development relies on genes/proteins which act as master regulators governing biofilm assembly. Thus, targeting these regulatory switches can effectively curb biofilm development. Phytochemicals have come up as a likely option that can be effective against biofilm-forming multi drug-resistant bacteria by interacting with biofilm forming master regulators. In this study, in silico approaches were implemented to compare the interacting efficiency of different phytochemicals on a master biofilm regulator protein in Escherichia coli (E. coli), a common SSI pathogen. Validation of the most potent phytochemicals after analyzing the in silico results were carried out under in vitro settings to confirm their antibacterial and antibiofilm potential against biofilm-forming bacteria. Furthermore, in vitro safety assessments on human embryonic kidney cells (HEK-293) demonstrated minimal cytotoxicity, confirming the bio-compatibility of the phytochemicals at the therapeutic concentrations. Thus, targeting central biofilm regulators with non-toxic phytochemicals may to reduce the incidence of biofilm associated infections in post-surgery patients.

candidates.title: Experimental and Pharmacoinformatic Studies Reveal Allium cepa L. Extract‐Mediated Modulation of Hepatitis B Virus Associated Inflammatory Pathways via Quercetin Glucoside Derivatives
candidates.authors: Gujarathi S, R. Harish D, Patil V, Karikazi A, Beerwala F, Chand J, Sahu G, Jalalpure S.
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTHepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health burden and often progresses to chronic liver inflammation, fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Although current antiviral therapies effectively suppress viral replication, their ability to modulate HBV‐associated complications remains limited. This study investigates the HBV‐associated antiviral and host modulatory potential of methanolic extract of Allium cepa bulb (AC) using integrated in vitro and computational approaches. Cytotoxicity, reverse transcriptase inhibition, time‐ and dose‐dependent inhibition of HBsAg and HBeAg levels, inflammatory cytokines, and specific host gene expression linked to HBV infections were assessed using HBV‐expressing HepG2.2.15 cells. LC‐MS detected phytocompounds were evaluated for their interaction with TLR4 using molecular docking and dynamics simulations using the Schrödinger suite. AC treatment reduced HBsAg and HBeAg levels up to 61.0% and 75.37%, respectively. Co‐treatment with Tenofovir alafenamide enhanced the inhibition to 79.0% and 94.55% without compromising cell viability. Among LC‐MS‐identified phytocompounds, computational analysis revealed stable interactions with Quercetin 3,4'‐diglucoside exhibiting the highest affinity (−14.23 kcal/mol) and maintaining stability with TLR4 throughout a 100 ns simulation. Overall, AC attenuated HBV‐induced inflammation through predicted modulation of TLR4‐mediated pathways and reduction of HBV antigen secretion, supporting its potential as a complementary therapeutic candidate for the management of chronic HBV infection.

candidates.title: Exploring molecular interactions between yeast topoisomerase I and RNA polymerase III subunit, Rpc82 using an in-silico approach
candidates.authors: Nandi P, Kamal I, Chakrabarti S, Sengupta S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractIntroductionThe process of DNA transcription leads to the generation of torsional stress, which must be resolved for smooth progression of the transcription machinery. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, DNA topoisomerase I (Top I), a type IB topoisomerase, plays a critical role in relaxing supercoils and mitigating the topological strain associated with transcription. While several proteins from the transcription machinery have been reported to interact with yeast Top I, the precise structural domains involved and the detailed features of the interaction interfaces remain largely unexplored. This gap is partly due to the absence of a complete three-dimensional structure of the full-length enzyme, which hinders structure-based computational analyses of its interactome.MethodsA full-length model of yeast Top I was generated using a domain-based modeling approach and evaluated using structural validation metrics and comparative analyses with homologous structures. Leveraging this model, we investigated a potential interaction between Top I and Rpc82, a key subunit of RNA polymerase III involved in transcription of small non-coding RNAs such as tRNAs and 5S rRNA. The interaction was evaluated using an integrative computational approach combining molecular docking, binding free-energy calculations, and molecular dynamics simulations. ResultsThe analyses identified a putative interaction interface involving the WH2–WH3 region of Rpc82 and primarily the D1 and D3 domains of Top I. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that the predicted Top I–Rpc82 complex remained structurally stable under the simulated conditions. The calculated binding energy-to-surface-area ratio of the complex was comparable to benchmark values for biologically relevant heterodimeric protein interfaces, supporting the plausibility of the predicted interaction.Discussion/ConclusionsOverall these findings provide a structural framework for future experimental validation of Top I interactions, paving the way for mechanistic insights into its regulatory functions and contribution to genome maintenance and stability.Keywords: protein-protein interaction, RNA polymerase III, Rpc82, topoisomerase I, transcription-topology connection

candidates.title: Functional assessment of CELSR1 variants associated with human developmental defects
candidates.journal: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
candidates.authors: Stenson J, Giang W, Latario S, Williams C, Trujillo Adorno V, Sha C, Stahley S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractDuring development, collective and oriented cell behaviors that drive organ formation and tissue patterning require coordination among neighboring cells governed by the highly conserved planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway. Deficiencies in PCP gene function result in severe developmental defects in model systems from flies to mice, while PCP gene mutations are associated with human birth defects impacting the neural tube and heart. Atypical cadherin Celsr1 engages in cell-cell adhesion to coordinate the asymmetric localization of Fz6 and Vangl2 to opposing sides of the PCP junction between neighboring cells. However, whether CELSR1 genetic variations disrupt function or contribute to disease pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Using cell-based assays for Celsr1 function, along with in silico modeling, we test a cohort of 17 Celsr1 mutations previously identified in patients with neural tube and congenital heart defects. In junctional enrichment assays, we find 13 variants displayed altered enrichment at cell borders relative to WT, including both loss- and gain-of-function behaviors. Further analysis of select Celsr1 mutations revealed defects in membrane mobility and perturbed co-recruitment of PCP protein Fz6. Our findings link Celsr1 mutations associated with human birth defects to functional defects in adhesion and PCP. In addition, our approach supports a framework for evaluating PCP function alongside genomics and in silico predictions toward understanding the pathophysiology impacts of genetic variations associated with human developmental disorders and gaining insight into Celsr1 function during development.Keywords: cadherin, cell adhesion, CELSR1, congenital heart defect, neural tube defect, PCP, planar cell polarity, variant pathogenicity

candidates.title: In silico evaluation of potential penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2) inhibitors from Borassus flabellifer haustorium against cephalosporin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae
candidates.authors: Rajasekaran U, Sridharan T.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackgroundThe emergence of cephalosporin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains, encoding altered Penicillin-Binding Protein 2 (PBP2), has become a major global public health concern. The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance necessitates the development of novel antimicrobial agents. In the present study, phytocompounds derived from the haustorium of Borassus flabellifer L. were investigated as potential inhibitors of PBP2 using an integrated in silico approach.MethodologyPhytochemical profiling of the methanol, ethyl acetate and hexane extracts of white spongy palmyra haustorium was performed using GC–MS and the identified compounds were subsequently evaluated for molecular docking, ADMET analysis and molecular dynamics simulation.ResultsA total of 69 compounds were identified and subjected to molecular docking against the transpeptidase domain of PBP2. The docking analysis revealed predicted binding affinities, ranging from −4.5 to −9.7 kcal/mol. The top ten compounds were subsequently evaluated for their ADMET and drug-likeness properties. Among these, 5-(4-nitrophenyl)-1,3,4-oxadiazol-2(5H)-one and 1,2,4-triazol-3-amine, 5-(1,3,5-trimethyl-4-pyrazolyl)amino, demonstrated comparatively favourable pharmacokinetic properties and balanced predicted ADMET profile. Furthermore, the stability of the complexes was assessed for a time period of 100 ns using molecular dynamics simulation. RMSD, RMSF, Rg, SASA, and hydrogen bonds were examined to evaluate protein-ligand interactions throughout the time frame. Principal component analysis and free energy landscape studies further supported ligand-induced stabilization of the PBP2 structure. MM-PBSA revealed favourable interaction energies of −19.11 ± 2.29 kJ/mol and −11.16 ± 2.34 kJ/mol for the two selected compounds, respectively. Among them, 5-(4-nitrophenyl)-1,3,4-oxadiazol-2(5H)-one demonstrated comparatively greater binding stability and thermodynamic favourability.ConclusionThese findings suggest that 5-(4-nitrophenyl)-1,3,4-oxadiazol-2(5H)-one could serve as a promising lead molecule for the development of new therapeutics against drug-resistant gonococcal infections and necessitate further experimental validation.Keywords: antimicrobial resistance, Borassus flabellifer haustorium, molecular dynamics simulation, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2)

candidates.title: Insights into Inhibitory Effects of Lapachol against Zika Virus
candidates.authors: Borjas Reyes S, Cassani N, Rodrigues Dutra J, Trevisan Aguillar da Silva M, Mesquita N, Martins Mota C, Mineo T, Oliva G, Guido R, Meireles B, Pandeló José D, Gomes Jardim A.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe reemergence of Zika virus (ZIKV) in 2015 and its association with severe neurological manifestations highlighted the urgent need for effective antiviral therapies, which, despite extensive efforts, remain unavailable. Lapachol, a 1,4-naphthoquinone compound abundant in Brazilian plant species, seems to be a promising candidate as an antiviral agent since its activity against other RNA viruses, as well as other human pathogens, including reported activity against Epstein–Barr virus and inhibition of herpes simplex virus type 1 by a lapachol-derived compound. Here, we investigated the activity of lapachol in inhibiting ZIKV replication by employing the wild-type strain ZIKVPE243. Lapachol exhibited potent inhibition of ZIKV with an EC50 of 3 μM and selectivity index of 50. Mechanistic assays suggest that its main action is exerted through postentry inhibition of viral replication, possibly through the blockage of the catalytic sites of NS2B-NS3 protease and NS5 polymerase. Biochemical enzymatic assays confirmed that lapachol inhibits NS2B-NS3 protease and NS5 polymerase activities, being complemented by molecular docking analyses. A protective effect was noted when cells were treated prior to infection, and lapachol was found to induce ROS formation in vitro, indicating that several antiviral mechanisms may be involved, including the initiation of an oxidative stress response that can affect viral particles. Overall, these findings shed light on the potential of lapachol to be used for the development of ZIKV inhibitors, especially targeting postentry stages of virus replication.

candidates.title: Investigating potential molecular mechanisms linking 6PPD-quinone exposure to Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: A network toxicology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulation study
candidates.authors: Yang B, Wang X, Zhuo L, Chen Y, He Q.
candidates.abstract: AbstractAs an emerging pollutant derived from tire rubber, 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q) has raised public health concerns due to widespread environmental exposure; however, its potential toxicological effects on avascular tissues such as intervertebral discs remain unclear. This study integrated network toxicology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation to investigate the potential mechanisms linking 6PPD-Q exposure to intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). ADMET toxicological predictions indicated high model-predicted probabilities for SR-MMP and SR-ARE activation. Through multidimensional database integration, 59 common targets potentially associated with 6PPD-Q and IVDD were identified. Protein–protein interaction network analysis further identified five hub genes: PTGS2, MMP2, SMAD3, RELA, and GSK3B. Functional enrichment analysis suggested that these targets were mainly involved in AGE-RAGE, PI3K-Akt, MAPK, TNF, and IL-17 signaling pathways, collectively implicating oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis. Molecular docking showed favorable predicted binding between 6PPD-Q and the five hub proteins, with RELA exhibiting the most favorable docking score (−8.82 kcal/mol). candidates.title: Luteolin protects against cholestasis by suppressing hepatocyte apoptosis through direct PI3K binding and AKT activation
candidates.authors: Zhao X, Xu Y, Liang H, Ji P, Li S, Wang S, Guo X, Zhang J.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackgroundExcessive hepatocyte apoptosis triggered by toxic bile acids is the core pathological event of cholestasis, and the direct target of luteolin (Lut), the major bioactive constituent of Siphonostegia chinensis Benth., for this protective effect remains unclear. This study aims to elucidate how Lut suppresses hepatocyte apoptosis and ameliorates cholestatic liver injury.MethodsA murine cholestasis model was induced by α-naphthylisothiocyanate (ANIT), and the hepatocyte apoptotic pathways were validated in glycochenodeoxycholic acid (GCDCA)-treated HepG2 cells. Liver tissue pathological changes were assessed via hematoxylin-eosin (HE) histological staining. Network pharmacology paired with supplementary RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) was used to screen candidate pathways contributing to Lut’s anti-cholestatic effects. Quantitative real-time PCR, Western blotting and Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) immunostaining were jointly utilized to assess apoptotic levels in liver parenchymal cells. Additionally, surface plasmon resonance (SPR) coupled with molecular docking simulations was adopted to clarify the direct binding profile of Lut.ResultsLut treatment markedly ameliorated serum biochemical indices and liver histopathological lesions in ANIT-exposed mice. Meanwhile, oxidative stress was alleviated, bile acid transporters were restored, inflammatory cytokines declined, and hepatocyte apoptosis was suppressed. Network pharmacology combined with RNA-seq predicted that Lut alleviates cholestasis through the Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/Protein Kinase B (PI3K/AKT)-mediated anti-apoptotic pathway. This hypothesis was further supported by TUNEL, Western blotting, and qRT-PCR analyses, which indicated that Lut could activate the PI3K/AKT, and then suppress hepatocyte apoptosis in cholestasis. SPR analysis revealed a concentration-dependent direct interaction between Lut and PI3K with a kinetic KD of 9.036 × 10−5 M, and molecular docking revealed a plausible binding mode within the kinase domain. Additionally, the anti-apoptotic effect of Lut was largely abolished when PI3K was inhibited by LY294002 in vitro.ConclusionThis study is the first to confirm that Lut directly targets PI3K to initiate the PI3K/AKT signaling cascade, and thereby suppresses bile acid-induced hepatocyte apoptosis. These findings refine the mechanistic understanding of Lut’s hepatoprotective action from general antioxidant activity to target-specific anti-apoptotic signaling, and provide a molecular explanation for the traditional use of S. chinensis Benth. for the treatment of damp-heat jaundice.Keywords: apoptosis, cholestasis, luteolin, PI3K/AKT pathway, Siphonostegia chinensis Benth., surface plasmon resonance

candidates.authors: Li S, Pan J, Lin L, Hong L, Li E, Zeng Y, Xu L, Dong G.
candidates.abstract: AbstractEzrin, a key member of the ERM (Ezrin–Radixin–Moesin) family, links the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton and is regulated by a conformational switch between closed and open states. Although phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate binding and phosphorylation at Thr567 are known to promote Ezrin activation, the associated conformational mechanism remains incompletely understood. Here, we combined Martini coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations with enhanced sampling, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, and MM/PBSA calculations to compare wild-type Ezrin with the phosphomimetic T567D mutant. The simulations indicate that T567 phosphorylation destabilizes the FERM/C-ERMAD interface, promotes domain separation, and facilitates exposure of membrane- and actin-binding sites. Computational analysis of binding free energies further demonstrates that the interaction between FERM and C-ERMAD is attenuated due to the phosphorylation of T567. Finally, a stepwise dissociation mechanism for the C-ERMAD α-helices is proposed. These results support a model in which T567 phosphorylation primarily promotes the initial transition toward an open conformation, whereas complete unfolding and full activation likely require additional events, including PIP2 binding, recruitment of partner proteins, and interaction with actin filaments.

candidates.title: Protein Thioether Crosslinks Installed by a SPASM-Containing Radical SAM Enzyme from Methanogenic Archaea
candidates.authors: Dieter E, Woodard A, Green J, Xiong J, Guo Y, Broderick W, Mitchell D, Broderick J.
candidates.abstract: Cysteine is a vital amino acid with wide biological utility, serving functions in catalysis, ligand binding, and maintenance of protein structures. In a subset of natural products, termed ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs), multiple subclasses are defined by the enzymatic modification of cysteine residues to form thioether bridges. However, RiPPs are short peptides and experimental validation of enzymatically installed thioether crosslinks on large protein substrates is limited. We hypothesized that cysteine-rich proteins whose genes are adjacent to those for enzymes predicted to catalyze RiPP-like modifications might be substrates for such modifications. Thus, we set out to investigate cysteine-rich prokaryotic proteomes for such examples. A bioinformatic analysis identified methanogenic archaea as suitable candidates for further investigation due to the high overall proteome cysteine content, and through targeted proteome scanning, we identified a suitable biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC; Crp) from Methanococcus voltae to characterize. Purification and reconstitution of an annotated radical S-adenosyl-l-methionine (RS) enzyme, CrpC, confirmed that the protein binds three [4Fe-4S] clusters, two of which are in a SPASM domain. Enzyme assays determined that CrpC is active after reconstitution and modifies a cysteine-rich protein substrate in the same BGC, CrpA. Mass spectrometry and chemical derivatization of modified CrpA indicates that CrpC installs ranthionine crosslinks onto CrpA. This research provides a new path for the discovery of intriguing BGCs and post-translational modifications and provides a foundation for the complete structural elucidation and assessment of the native biological function of these modified cysteine-rich proteins.

candidates.title: Protein–Protein Interface Residue Prediction by Integrating Protein Language Representations and Structural Graph Attention
candidates.authors: Hou Z, He W, Cao W, Li J, Li H, Sun S, Yang H.
candidates.abstract: Accurate residue-level prediction of protein–protein interaction interfaces is important for elucidating molecular recognition mechanisms and guiding targeted drug design. However, interface residues are relatively sparse and governed by complex spatial dependencies, making their accurate identification challenging. In this study, we developed EvoStruct-GAT, a multimodal graph attention model based on the PDBbind v2020.R1 data set. To reduce information leakage arising from sequence homology, receptor and ligand sequences were clustered independently, and the resulting clusters were used to construct training, validation, and test sets with no overlap in either receptor or ligand clusters. EvoStruct-GAT represents the target protein as a residue-level graph and integrates ESM-2 protein language model representations, DSSP-derived structural descriptors, and distance-aware graph attention, together with a combined strategy for addressing class imbalance. Using a minimum cross-partner heavy-atom distance of less than 5 Å to define interface residues, the model achieved an AUROC of 0.8081, an AUPRC of 0.4475, and an F1 score of 0.4562 on the independent test set. Alternative labels based on 4.0 Å, 4.5 Å, and ΔSASA definitions produced comparable AUROC values, indicating that the residue-ranking capability was reasonably robust across the tested interface definitions. Ablation experiments identified ESM-2 representations as the principal contributor to performance, with DSSP information and inter-residue message passing providing additional value. Under a common evaluation protocol, EvoStruct-GAT outperformed simplified internal baselines and showed complementary performance characteristics in external comparisons with publicly available models. These results demonstrate that EvoStruct-GAT can effectively rank potential interface residues without requiring information about a known binding partner, thereby supporting candidate-site selection, experimental validation, and downstream structural and functional analyses.

candidates.abstract: Helicobacter pylori is a major human pathogen associated with gastric cancer and a growing global public health concern due to increasing antimicrobial resistance. As H. pylori lacks de novo purine biosynthesis and relies entirely on purine salvage for nucleotide production, purine nucleoside phosphorylase represents a rational antibacterial target. Natural products remain a valuable and largely underexplored source of structurally diverse scaffolds for the discovery of novel enzyme inhibitors, with marine organisms representing a rich yet underexploited source of such bioactive metabolites; however, the pharmacological exploration of this enzyme from natural sources remains limited. In this context, six terpenoids, including five brominated diterpenes, isolated from the red macroalga Sphaerococcus coronopifolius were screened against recombinant H. pylori PNP using a target-based biochemical approach. Two of the six compounds tested, bromosphaerol and sphaerodactylomelol, showed reproducible inhibitory activity at 30 μM, reducing H. pylori PNP activity by 46.04 ± 4.70% and 39.39 ± 8.24%, respectively. Molecular docking predicted binding of both compounds within the active-site purine-binding region, with hydrophobic contacts involving Phe159 and Leu206. Hydrogen bonds were predicted with the backbone carbonyl of Ile178 for bromosphaerol and of Phe159 for sphaerodactylomelol. Molecular dynamics simulations (200 ns, three independent replicates per system) showed that both ligands remained stably accommodated within the predicted active-site binding pocket across all six monomers of the hexameric assembly, while root mean square deviation (RMSD) and root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) analyses indicated that the enzyme retained its global structural integrity throughout the simulations. Bromosphaerol exhibited a lower RMSD than the conformationally flexible sphaerodactylomelol, reflecting differences in ligand dynamics within the binding pocket. Taken together, these findings provide initial biochemical evidence that S. coronopifolius represents a source of secondary metabolites capable of interacting with H. pylori PNP, and nominate bromosphaerol and sphaerodactylomelol as preliminary hits for future concentration–response characterization.

In addition to CYP-mediated bioactivation, DDS may contribute to lysosomal stress-associated iron imbalance and oxidative propagation. Conventional antioxidants or iron-chelating therapies alone may provide only partial protection against these interconnected mechanisms. This study evaluated the protective effects of α-lipoic acid (ALA) and deferoxamine (DFO), administered individually or in combination, against DDS-induced oxidative and hematological disturbances using integrated in vivo and in silico approaches. Male Swiss mice received DDS (40 mg/kg, gavage) for 5 days, followed by treatment with ALA (25 mg/kg, gavage), DFO (40 mg/kg, i.p.), or their combination for an additional 5 days. Methemoglobin (MetHb), reduced glutathione (GSH), nitric oxide (NO), malondialdehyde (MDA), and plasma iron levels were evaluated. Histopathological analysis and molecular docking studies involving cytochrome P450 isoforms (CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A4, and CYP2E1) and hemoglobin were performed to investigate potential mechanisms underlying DDS-induced toxicity and the protective effects of ALA and DFO. DDS markedly increased MetHb, nitric oxide, malondialdehyde, and plasma iron levels, accompanied by depletion of GSH and hepatocellular degeneration. ALA and DFO individually attenuated oxidative and iron-related disturbances, whereas combined treatment effectively reduced methemoglobin formation and preserved hepatic architecture; however, plasma ferric iron levels remained comparable to those in DDS-treated animals. Molecular docking suggested preferential interactions of DDS with CYP2E1 and CYP3A4, supporting the biological plausibility of their involvement in oxidative bioactivation pathways, whereas DFO showed predicted interactions with CYP2C9, CYP2E1, and hemoglobin-associated iron sites. Collectively, these findings indicate that ALA and DFO each attenuate DDS-induced hepatotoxicity and hematotoxicity through distinct but complementary antioxidant, iron-chelating, and redox-modulating mechanisms. Combined treatment effectively improved selected endpoints, including methemoglobin formation and hepatic architecture, although its protective effects were endpoint-dependent. The molecular modeling results provide supportive mechanistic insights and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating evidence complementary to the in vivo findings.

candidates.title: 1H, 13C, and 15N chemical shift assignments of monomorphic Aβ1-40 at 100 kHz MAS in a diamond rotor
candidates.abstract: Abstract Amyloid-β (Aβ) fibrils are the principal component of the senile plaques that characterize Alzheimer's disease, and fibrils formed from the Aβ 1−40 alloform are strongly polymorphic, which has long complicated their structural characterization. We recently reported a reproducible, unseeded, monomorphic Aβ 1−40 fibril grown at neutral pH from supersaturated monomer, together with its atomic-resolution structure and its 13 C and 15 N chemical shift assignments (PDB 12GB; BMRB 31300). Here we extend that reference to 1 H. From a 3D 1 H-detected hCCH (RFDR) experiment and a 2D hNH experiment recorded at 18.8 T and ω r /2π = 100 kHz on approximately 0.5 mg of hydrated fibrils packed in a home-built 0.7 mm single-crystal diamond rotor, we assign 123 1 H resonances, corresponding close to 90% of the distinct 1 H sites of the rigid core (residues Q15→V40), together with sixteen 1 H of the dynamic N-terminal segment. The 1 H-detected data additionally yield six previously unassigned 13 C and three previously unassigned 15 N resonances, predominantly in aromatic side chains and in the mobile N-terminus, and nine 1 H- 13 C and twenty 1 H- 15 N inter-residue contacts that are consistent with the published structure. These assignments provide a residue-level reference for fingerprinting Aβ 1−40 polymorphs and for mapping the binding of antibodies, chaperones and small molecules to this fibril.

candidates.title: A Bispecific Biologic That Robustly Reverses HIV-1 and SIV Latency
candidates.abstract: AbstractAntiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV-1 replication but cannot eliminate the latent viral reservoir persisting in memory CD4 T cells. Existing latency reversal candidates have yet to achieve robust viral reactivation at tolerable doses. We engineered T4IL15Δ, a bispecific biologic that selectively delivers IL-15 signaling to memory CD4 T cells, with minimal off-target stimulation. T4IL15Δ reactivated latent virus in 94% (48/51) of clinical samples ex vivo, 75% (15/20) of administrations in HIV-1-infected and ART-suppressed humanized mice, and 100% (6/6) of SIV-infected and ART-suppressed rhesus macaques at doses well tolerated. We also found that off-target stimulation of non-CD4 cells hindered HIV-1 reactivation ex vivo. T4IL15Δ provides a robust reactivation platform that could complement other reservoir-elimination strategies toward an HIV-1 cure.

candidates.title: A bacterial endosymbiont with a highly reduced genome forms extensive membrane contact sites with host organelles
candidates.abstract: SUMMARY Bacterial endosymbionts that establish long-term associations inside of host cells often lose a huge number of genes and become dependent on their hosts for essential cellular functions 1,2 . One such example is the mealybug endosymbiont Tremblaya princeps : its ~139-kb genome encodes only ~120 protein coding genes and lacks all recognizable genes for lipid and fatty acid synthesis, cell wall components, membrane transport, protein translocation, and transmembrane proteins, raising fundamental questions of how Tremblaya’s cellular envelope is formed and maintained 3,4 . Here, using a combination of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) of an entire endosymbiont-containing insect cell, we identified extensive and specific contacts between host cell mitochondria and Tremblaya . These contacts occurred at close membrane appositions and contained electron-dense bridge-like structures closely resembling classical eukaryotic membrane contact sites. Whole-cell segmentation showed that approximately 53% of host mitochondria were in contact with Tremblaya , with some mitochondria extensively wrapped by Tremblaya -associated membranes. Mitochondria in contact with Tremblaya were larger and contained proportionally greater cristae volume and surface density compared to non-contact mitochondria, exhibiting differences in both external and internal mitochondrial architecture. As membrane contact sites are well known to mediate lipid and metabolite exchange between membranes 5–10 , these findings suggest that direct interactions with host organelles may be a source of vital membrane and cellular components for endosymbionts that have lost the autonomous ability to produce and transport these molecules.

candidates.title: A minimally modified AAV9 variant (AAV9fyhr) for enhanced CNS gene delivery by intra-CSF administration
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTAdeno-associated virus (AAV) mediated gene therapies continue to show promise for the treatment of genetic diseases. However, delivery and safety still represent significant prohibitive barriers restricting translation of these delivery modalities to humans. We describe a novel AAV9 variant, “AAV9fyhr” or “FYHR”, identified from screening a controlled randomization point mutation AAV9 library in mice and nonhuman primates followed by directed evolution of in vivo CNS-derived libraries screened in human iPSC differentiated cortical neurons. Capsid variants of interest were identified by coupling long read sequencing and computational structure modeling. Structure-function analysis of our lead candidate reveal that two targeted amino acid changes are sufficient to result in beneficial pleiotropic effects across viral stability, cell surface attachment, and gene delivery. We developed a novel multiplexed barcoding reporter system, enabling a time and cost-effective option to gather spatially resolved single cell capsid validation data in mice and nonhuman primates. When administered intrathecally, AAV9fyhr exhibits 2-to-6-fold higher gene delivery across several tissues in the CNS while minimally altering the tropism to peripheral tissues in comparison to AAV9. These findings demonstrate the potential of whole capsid engineering for the rational development of translational next generation AAV capsids.

candidates.title: A transient third metal ion shapes the catalytic cycle of a group I intron ribozyme
candidates.abstract: Abstract The self-splicing group I intron ribozyme from Tetrahymena thermophillia (THr) is a prototypical example of how RNA overcomes its limited chemical repertoire to form complex, negatively charged junctions and catalyze chemical reactions. Despite over 30 years of bio-chemical and structural characterization, questions still remain regarding the requirements for THr catalysis that may inform structure based drug design against group I introns, as well as the use of THr as an RNA editing tool. Recent cryo-EM structures have provided an unprecedented window into the first and second steps of splicing, enabling detailed mechanistic investigation at the atomistic level. In this work, we leverage solvation theory, molecular dynamics, alchemical free energy simulations, and machine learning accelerated QM/MM to probe outstanding questions related to 1) the role of a possible third Mg 2+ binding in the active site, 2) differences in catalytic requirements between G exo cofactors and between the first and second steps of splicing, 3) the potential role of an acid or base, and 4) restrictions on the identity of the 5 ′ exon splice site nucleotide, U(−1). We propose that a transient, cofactor dependent, interaction with a third metal participates in the first step, while a higher affinity interaction with this third ion is required in the second step. We also propose that the presence of a phosphate on the G exo in the first step, and analogously the G ω in the second step, forms a metal ion binding site not present when guanosine is bound. Finally, we propose and computationally test design modifications of G22 (isofunctional substitutions of 2,6-diaminopurine that tune the p K a at the N1 position) that we predict will enable the accommodation of C(–1) in a crucial wobble-like pair at physiological pH. This design would provide a potential strategy for expanding the sequence space accessible to programmable trans-splicing ribozymes in RNA editing applications. TOC Graphic

candidates.title: An Expanded Lpt Pathway Couples Surface Lipoprotein Export to Outer Membrane Vesicle Biogenesis in Bacteroides
candidates.abstract: Abstract The ecological dominance of Bacteroidota in the human gut microbiota derives from their exceptional capacity to metabolize diverse dietary and host-derived glycans. This ability relies on surface-exposed lipoproteins (SLPs), which are displayed on the bacterial surface and selectively packaged into outer membrane vesicles (OMVs). Although SLP export and OMV biogenesis are tightly coupled, the mechanism linking these processes has remained unknown. Here, we identify LptZ, a previously uncharacterized protein, as a critical link between SLP surface translocation and OMV biogenesis. Cryo-electron tomography of the lptZ mutant revealed chains of vesicles tethered to the outer membrane, offering a rare glimpse into an arrested stage of OMV formation in which vesicle fission is impaired. Proteomic analysis further showed that, in the absence of LptZ, a subset of SLPs fails to reach the cell surface and instead accumulates at the inner membrane. Unexpectedly, LptZ associates with the lipopolysaccharide transport (Lpt) machinery and repurposes it for SLP translocation. Crosslinking experiments revealed selective associations between multiple SLPs and Lpt proteins, providing mechanistic evidence for the direct involvement of the Lpt machinery in SLP trafficking. We further show that the Bacteroides Lpt machinery contains previously unrecognized components, revealing an unanticipated level of specialization relative to canonical Lpt systems. Together, our findings uncover a previously unknown protein export pathway, expand the functional role of the Lpt machinery, and establish a direct mechanistic link between SLP translocation and OMV biogenesis in Bacteroidota.

candidates.title: An ancestral tRNA maturation enzyme repurposed for cytoplasmic non-coding RNA processing
candidates.abstract: Abstract Ribonuclease Z enzymes remove 3′ trailers from precursor tRNAs. In human cells, ELAC2/RNase Z L matures nuclear and mitochondrial pre-tRNAs, whereas the cytosolic short paralog ELAC1/RNase Z S repairs ANKZF1-cleaved tRNAs, but its broader substrate repertoire remains unclear. We investigated ELAC1 function using transcriptome profiling, small RNA sequencing, CLIP-seq, and biochemical reconstitution. ELAC1 was dispensable for canonical tRNA processing but associated with structured RNA polymerase III transcripts, prominently Y RNAs and vault RNAs (vtRNAs). Purified ELAC1 cleaved all four human vtRNAs near their 3′ ends, with high-resolution mapping identifying a conserved cleavage position within the 3′ extension. Efficient cleavage required structural features of the vtRNA terminal region. In contrast, ELAC2 showed little or no vtRNA cleavage under the conditions tested and displayed stricter substrate and cleavage-site selection on pre-tRNA. Loss and re-expression of ELAC1 altered structured ncRNA abundance and small-RNA end profiles. These findings identify vtRNAs as direct ELAC1 substrates and support functional specialization of human ELAC paralogs, with ELAC2 favoring precise pre-tRNA maturation and ELAC1 exhibiting broader RNA substrate specificity.

candidates.title: Asymmetric assembly underlies activation mechanism of neuronal GIRK1/2 channels
candidates.abstract: AbstractG protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK; Kir3) channels are principal effectors of inhibitory GPCR signaling. Here we combine cryo-electron microscopy, single-molecule imaging, electrophysiology and molecular dynamics to define the architecture and activation of neuronal GIRK1/2 channels. GIRK1/2 preferentially assembles as an asymmetric heterotetramer containing one GIRK1 and three GIRK2 subunits. Three PIP₂ molecules bound to GIRK2 promote partial cytoplasmic-domain docking, whereas engagement of a fourth PIP₂ by GIRK1 completes docking and opens the helix bundle crossing gate. GIRK1 also remodels the electrostatic environment beneath the selectivity filter, where its E141 and D173 residues create a permeation module that enhances K⁺ conduction. The GIRK1-selective activator ML297 binds at the GIRK1–GIRK2 interface and controls both permeation and gating. These findings establish how asymmetric assembly couples sequential lipid-dependent gating to efficient K⁺ permeation and GIRK1-dependent pharmacological activation.

candidates.title: BCKDK Inhibitors Directly Antagonize Angiotensin II Type 1 Receptor and Induce Vasodilation Independently of BCAA Catabolism or BCKDK
candidates.abstract: AbstractBranched-chain amino acids (BCAA) have been implicated in diabetes and heart failure, leading to ongoing clinical trials with inhibitors of BCKDK, a key regulator of BCAA catabolism. We have previously shown that these inhibitors promote vasodilation and lower blood pressure, well-known cardioprotective effects, but how this occurs remained unclear. We show here, using explanted vessels, in vivo hemodynamics and telemetry, and genetically modified mice, that the vasodilatory effect of BCKDK inhibitors is direct, rapid, independent of nitric oxide, independent of BCAA catabolism, and most strikingly, independent of BCKDK itself. Instead, we demonstrate, using structural and biochemical studies, that BCKDK inhibitors directly antagonize the angiotensin II type I receptor (AT1R) and consequent angiotensin-mediated vasoconstriction. These data demonstrate a strong off-target effect of BCKDK inhibitors, independent of BCAA or BCKDK, which may explain their cardioprotective effects but also questions if this protection would be additive to existing AT1R blockers.
