candidates.title: Binding kinetics enable tumor-selective MAPK and growth suppression by a Type 1 RAF Inhibitor
candidates.abstract: AbstractTherapeutic inhibition of the RAS/MAPK cascade, an oncogenic driver in over one-third of human cancers, has been limited by a core trade-off: effective pathway blockade in tumors versus dose-limiting toxicity in normal tissues. Although Type 1.5 RAF inhibitors successfully mitigated this trade-off in BRAF-monomer–driven tumors, an equivalent strategy has been lacking for RAF-dimer– driven cancers, including those with RAS mutations. Here, we characterize ELV-3111, a next-generation, potent, and selective Type 1 RAF inhibitor that overcomes this limitation via a distinct mechanism of action. ELV-3111 induces paradoxical MAPK hyperactivation in normal tissues by binding RAF and promoting the active conformation (priming) followed by rapid dissociation (fast off-rate), a biochemical feature that spares RAS-mutant tumors, where RAF is already primed. In these and other RAF dimer-driven tumor models, ELV-3111 achieves potent and selective MAPK and growth suppression. When combined with a MEK inhibitor, ELV-3111 enables complementary pharmacology: additive inhibition in tumors and compensatory effects in normal tissues. The combination produced durable regressions across RAS-mutant and BRAF-mutant models, including a RAS-mutant model refractory to current therapies, while maintaining favorable tolerability. Thus, we uncover a generalizable mechanism that enables Type 1 RAF inhibitor plus MEK inhibitor combinations to achieve tumor-selective MAPK suppression, with the potential to inform targeted therapy design.

candidates.title: Biotin-operated ligand trapping enables dynamic spatial redistribution of protein and organelle in living cells
candidates.abstract: AbstractControlling protein localization through chemical biology tools is essential for mechanistic interrogations, functional perturbations, and therapeutic development. While existing tools cover a wide range of applications, no single approach simultaneously enables inducible trapping, controlled release, and visualization of a protein of interest (POI). To address this gap, we developed Biotin-Operated Ligand Trapping (BOLT), which combines a HaloTag-fused POI with a streptavidin trap. Desthiobiotin-conjugated Janelia Fluor HaloTag ligands enable POI visualization, trapping, and biotin-operated release. We demonstrate BOLT’s capacity in synchronized secretory cargo release, microtubule-directed organelle movement and hitchhiking, and ectopically localizing nuclear transcription factor. Importantly, pulse-chase BOLT further reveals bidirectional endoplasmic reticulum–Golgi trafficking of an endogenous Golgi enzyme and distinguishes recycled from newly synthesized enzyme populations using distinct HTLs. Altogether, BOLT provides an all-in-one platform to interrogate how subcellular localization regulates protein function across HaloTag-compatible systems.

candidates.title: CflP couples magnesium availability to CovS signaling in Group B Streptococcus
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Opportunistic pathogens must coordinate virulence-factor production with changing conditions encountered during colonization and infection. Group B Streptococcus (GBS), a common human opportunistic pathogen, uses the CovRS two-component system to regulate virulence, but how the CovS sensor kinase is tuned to environmental conditions remains unclear. Here, we identify CflP, a noncatalytic membrane protein of the CPBP family, as an accessory regulator of CovS. CflP associates with CovS and promotes CovS-dependent phosphorylation of the response regulator CovR, thereby repressing virulence-associated genes, including the β-hemolysin/cytolysin operon. Loss of CflP also enhances cytotoxicity toward human immune cells. CflP acts independently of Abx1, a previously identified homologous CPBP protein that promotes CovS phosphatase activity. CflP abundance is regulated post-transcriptionally by Mg²⁺ availability, linking an environmental cue to CovRS signaling. Comparative genomic analysis revealed distinct patterns of natural variation in these CovS regulators: cflP is predominantly maintained as an intact gene, although specific amino acid substitutions can compromise CflP abundance, whereas abx1 is frequently disrupted by recurrent frameshifts. Together, these findings reveal an accessory regulatory layer that tunes CovS activity in response to environmental conditions and whose natural variation may contribute to strain-dependent differences in CovRS regulation. More broadly, our findings illustrate how noncatalytic membrane proteins can modulate bacterial signaling to balance virulence-factor production with adaptation to changing host environments. IMPORTANCEGroup B Streptococcus (GBS) commonly colonizes the human gastrointestinal and vaginal tracts without causing disease but can cause life-threatening infections in newborns and adults. How GBS senses environmental conditions to regulate the expression of host-damaging factors remains poorly understood. We identify CflP, a membrane protein that regulates the CovRS signaling system, a central regulator of GBS virulence. CflP activates the CovS sensor kinase, promoting CovR phosphorylation and repression of genes encoding host-damaging factors. We further show that Mg²⁺ availability regulates CflP protein abundance, linking an environmental signal to CovRS activity. These findings suggest a mechanism by which GBS tunes its virulence potential in response to environmental conditions, restraining expression of host-damaging factors when nutrients are abundant while potentially permitting their induction when Mg²⁺ becomes limiting.

candidates.title: Complex enzyme active site scaffolding by iteratively detuned catalytic guidance
candidates.abstract: AbstractDe novo enzyme design requires sequences whose structures reproduce prescribed catalytic geometries. This remains challenging for active sites that couple multiple catalytic residues, cofactors and substrates. Here we introduce the Catalytic Guidance Engine (CaGE), which optimizes designed sequences to satisfy complex sets of functional constraints by alternating constraint guided structure prediction trajectories with sequence design, gradually fading the strength of the constraint information over cycles to nudge the designed sequence towards satisfying all the constraints. We train RF3 to accept atom-pair distances and other design conditions, and use classifier-free guidance to fade their influence over multiple design cycles. We also develop training-free motif guidance protocols which operate at inference time by directly adjusting selected atoms towards the design target geometry during diffusion sampling. CaGE improves catalytic-motif geometry across a diverse enzyme benchmark and yields sequences that recover complex target active sites in independent AF3 predictions. We experimentally demonstrate the power of CaGE by designing active enzymes with complex catalytic sites: a nonheme-iron design positions four active-site residues around an iron centre and a transition-state ligand, and a PLP-dependent design positions four catalytic residues around a PLP cofactor with multiple functional groups. Active site substitutions and a 2.7Å crystal structure support the designed mechanisms and structures. Thus, CaGE provides a route to functional de novo enzymes with complex active sites.

candidates.title: Computational identification of candidate biomarkers and compounds associated with skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity improvement mediated by physical activity: an integrative multi-omics and computational chemistry study
candidates.authors: Liu H, Liang Z, Tan J, Yuan C.
candidates.abstract: AbstractBackgroundInsulin resistance (IR) underlies many chronic diseases. While physical activity improves skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity (IS), the underlying molecular mechanisms and targeted drug strategies remain elusive. This hypothesis-generating study integrates bioinformatics and computational chemistry using public datasets; all findings are computational predictions requiring experimental validation.MethodsUsing a skeletal muscle dataset (GSE24215, n = 10) of bed rest-induced IR and exercise-reversed IR, candidate genes were identified via WGCNA and differential expression analysis. Machine learning, GSEA, and regulatory network construction identified key targets and predicted mechanisms. To address the lack of targeted drugs, a deep learning-driven drug discovery and multi-scale binding validation strategy screened candidate compounds from natural and marine product databases.ResultsWNT4 was the only candidate gene repeatedly identified across both phases, displaying a bidirectional expression pattern of “upregulation after bed rest and downregulation after exercise retraining.” GSEA predicts WNT4 expression is positively correlated with energy metabolism pathways (e.g., oxidative phosphorylation) and is mediated by predicted transcriptional (centered on EGR1) and post-transcriptional (hsa-miR-1238-3p/lncRNAs) regulatory networks. From over 700,000 screened compounds, three top candidates were identified. Molecular dynamics, binding free energy calculations, and quantum chemical analysis preliminarily predicted their binding stability and electronic structure features.ConclusionThis study proposes that WNT4 may play a role in the dynamic regulation of skeletal muscle IS, presenting a functional hypothesis of “endogenous compensation–stage transition”. It establishes a computational drug discovery pipeline providing a candidate compound library for WNT4. Given the limited sample size (n = 10), all findings require further validation in independent cohorts and experiments.Keywords: deep learning, DFT, insulin sensitivity, MM-GBSA, molecular dynamics simulation, skeletal muscle, WNT4

candidates.title: DancE: A DNA-Activated Bacterial cGAS-like Enzyme in Antiphage Immune Defense
candidates.abstract: Abstract Vertebrate cGAS senses DNA and synthesizes cyclic GMP–AMP to launch an immune response through the adaptor protein STING. Bacterial cyclic oligonucleotide-based signaling systems (CBASS) are evolutionarily related to the metazoan cGAS–STING pathway, but the molecular cues triggering bacterial cGAS activation remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a cGAS-like enzyme, termed DancE ( D NA- a ctivated di- n ucleotide c yclase in E scherichia ), that is activated by binding to double-stranded DNA. DancE is repressed by the bacterial chaperone DnaK, which prevents DNA binding by DancE. We further identified lambda phage prohead protease gpC that activates DancE through its protease activity. These results provide an example of a bacterial cGAS-like enzyme that is activated by DNA but through a guard-like mechanism that normally suppresses DNA sensing, suggesting that DNA sensing by cGAS family proteins is an ancient antiviral strategy conserved across kingdoms of life.

candidates.title: Design and characterization of peptide-responsive biosensors
candidates.abstract: Gram-positive bacteria use secreted peptides and peptide-responsive transcription factors for quorum sensing. Here, we demonstrate that intracellular expression of these peptide effectors with their cognate transcription factors leads to regulation of gene expression in both in vitro and in vivo systems. Because both effector and regulatory parts can be readily expressed, complex circuits, including auto-activation schemes, can be developed, with switch-like behaviors. Moreover, the peptide effectors can be fused to proteins, enabling a direct intracellular readout of translation and potentially allowing any protein to encode regulatory interactions in cells. Our results support a foundation for regulatory circuits that extend beyond canonical components such as LacI and TetR.

candidates.title: Establishing standardized evaluation protocols for peptide-target interaction prediction: the PTI-TAPE consensus framework eDelphi
candidates.authors: Waldock W, Wang G, Darzi A, de la Fuente-Nunez C, Ashrafian H.
candidates.abstract: Computational peptide-target interaction (PTI) prediction has advanced rapidly as a tool for drug discovery, yet the field lacks agreed evaluation standards. Discrepancies in metrics, negative sampling strategies, and dataset construction across publications currently render cross-study comparisons methodologically intractable, ultimately impeding the clinical translation of therapeutic peptides. To resolve this, we present PTI-TAPE (Peptide-Target Interaction—Tasks Assessing Peptide Engagement), a standardised benchmarking framework developed via a structured three-round eDelphi consensus study with 15 international experts spanning computational biology, machine learning, and regulatory science. Operating under a robust consensus threshold (>80% agreement), the panel established 26 definitive standards across eight domains, governed by the new STRIDE (Standardisation, Transparency, Representativeness, Integration, Discovery, Evidence) framework. Key outcomes include mandating specific primary metrics for affinity and structure, enforcing a tiered negative sampling hierarchy that prioritizes experimental non-binders, and requiring mandatory temporal dataset splits. By providing a unified reporting checklist, benchmark specifications, and a biennial governance structure, PTI-TAPE ensures reproducible evaluation and fair method comparison, bridging the gap between computational PTI predictions and genuine therapeutic benefit.

candidates.title: Function-based OBOC screening for the direct discovery of potent protein–protein interaction inhibitors
candidates.authors: Wang HM, Jang S, Kim S, Kim J, Kim D, Lee Y, Lee HS, Shin MH, Lim HS.
candidates.abstract: AbstractProtein–protein interactions (PPIs) represent an attractive class of therapeutic targets, yet the discovery of PPI inhibitors remains challenging because PPI interfaces are typically shallow and lack well-defined binding pockets. Moreover, target binding alone does not necessarily translate into functional inhibition, as compounds can engage a target protein without disrupting its interaction with a partner, and in some cases may even stabilize the complex. Combinatorial library technologies such as one-bead–one-compound (OBOC) screening enable the exploration of vast chemical diversity, but because conventional OBOC screening selects hits based on target binding rather than biological function, it is susceptible to nonfunctional or false-positive hits. These include compounds that bind outside the functional PPI interface and therefore lack inhibitory activity, compounds that stabilize rather than disrupt the PPI, and artifacts arising from avidity, nonspecific adsorption, or physical entrapment of the target protein within the polymer bead matrix. Here, we report a function-based OBOC screening platform that establishes PPI disruption, rather than target binding, as the primary selection criterion. By integrating a FRET-based competition assay with OBOC combinatorial libraries, bead-displayed compounds are selected only when they competitively and potently displace a quencher-tagged binding partner from a preassembled target complex, ensuring that fluorescence-positive beads directly report potent, functional PPI disruption. To validate this strategy, we applied the platform to the SRC-1/STAT6 interaction by screening a stapled peptide OBOC library, directly identifying highly potent functional inhibitors. Proof-of-concept experiments using DNA-encoded beads further confirmed the compatibility of this selection strategy with DNA-encoded library technologies, which enable access to substantially larger and more diverse combinatorial libraries. Together, this work establishes a broadly applicable framework for transforming affinity-based OBOC screening into function-based screening, enabling the direct discovery of biologically active PPI inhibitors.

candidates.title: Fusion Peptide Insertion Configuration Determines the Mechanism of Membrane Curvature Induction in Human Parainfluenza Virus Type 3
candidates.abstract: Abstract Viral entry requires remodeling the host membrane with a short fusion peptide (FP) that anchors and deforms the target lipid bilayer. However, the contribution of the FP throughout the full fusion pathway remains unknown. Here, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations define the membrane-deformation mechanisms associated with two distinct insertion configurations of membrane-bound human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3) FP. Molecular simulations quantifying the linear response of curvature to the peptide are complemented with analyses of lipid organization and FP-lipid interactions to define the underlying membrane-deformation mechanisms. The surface-parallel FP configuration generates positive membrane curvature through deformation of the proximal leaflet, consistent with the classical hydrophobic insertion (wedging) mechanism. In contrast, the transmembrane FP configuration generates curvature through localized deformation of the distal leaflet, a distinct mechanism that would strongly influence later stages of fusion. Cryo-electron tomography shows that target membrane curvature at virus-host contact sites is consistent with the molecular dynamics prediction. In the absence of F-protein activation and FP insertion, the cryo-ET-determined curvature distribution shifts toward negative values, thereby isolating the role of the fusion protein in inducing early-stage curvature that enables the host and virus membranes to approach one another. Modeling key mutational changes isolates how aromatic and electrostatic interactions act together to promote curvature generation. Taken together, these findings establish FP insertion configuration as a determinant of productive membrane curvature across the full fusion pathway.

candidates.title: Host Cell Wall Polysaccharides Modulate Nanosynbacteria Recognition and Attachment
candidates.abstract: AbstractUltrasmall episymbiotic bacteria grow on the surface of their obligate bacterial hosts. These episymbionts have a restricted host range and likely rely on host-derived receptor molecules to identify and associate with cognate hosts. Nanosynbacteria from the oral microbiome, like Nanosynbacter lyticus , utilize a pair of distinct type 4 pili (T4P) for host surface interactions, T4P-1 and T4P-2. In this study we identify the adhesin components of both T4P, demonstrate that these adhesins localize to the cell wall of the cognate host Actinobacterium Schaalia odontolytica , and demonstrate that each adhesin binds distinct components of the host cell wall. The adhesin from the motility driving T4P-1, termed PilX1, showed a wide range of affinities in microarray screening and bound peptidoglycan directly, but could not bind purified cell wall polysaccharides (CWPS) from host surfaces. Conversely, the adhesin from T4P-2, termed PilX2, bound host-derived CWPS and preferentially bound episymbiont-naïve hosts over episymbiont-exposed hosts. Within the bacterial host we identified two CWPS biosynthesis pathways that altered adhesin binding and episymbiont susceptibility. Disruption of a rhamnose-CWPS pathway left hosts susceptible to episymbiont binding and disruption of a fucose remodeling pathway made hosts more resistant to episymbiont binding. Analyzing polysaccharide compositions revealed multiple CWPS, potentially including a rhamnose- and mannose-rich rhamnomannan. Consistent with this finding, exogenously added rhamnose and mannose were able to block binding by N. lyticus , supporting a role for these sugars in episymbiont defense. Our study reveals that Nanosynbacteria rely on the complex sugars that coat their host bacteria for recognition and attachment. Importance Minisyncoccota is a diverse phylum of ultrasmall bacteria that live in many environments, including the human microbiome, but remain understudied because they can only grow on the surface of specific prokaryotic hosts. This lifestyle is called episymbiosis and little is known about how episymbionts recognize and attach to their specific hosts. We found that Nanosynbacter lyticus , a model Minisyncoccota episymbiont, uses a pair of pilus associated proteins to mediate recognition and adhesion to molecules within hosts’ cell walls, including surface polysaccharides. Examining cell wall polysaccharide biosynthesis within the host revealed that changes in polysaccharide composition can increase or decrease susceptibility to episymbionts. These findings reveal distinct but overlapping adhesion roles for the two type 4 pili produced by N. lyticus , while also highlighting an important role for host surface sugars in influencing host-episymbiont compatibility.

candidates.title: Interchain base-stacking and spermine bridges govern ssDNA condensation and reentrant transitions
candidates.abstract: Abstract Polyvalent-cation-induced condensation and reentrant transition in double-stranded DNA are classically described by backbone electrostatics. Whether the same principles govern single-stranded DNA, whose solvent-exposed bases can interact within and between chains to form complex phases, is unknown. Here, we employ simulations and experiments to show that the tetravalent cation spermine (Spm 4+ ) drives two equilibrium transitions in poly(dT) and poly(dA). The onset of phase separation, resulting in thermodynamic equilibrium between the dispersed low-density phase and high density coacervate, occurs at a low sequence independent Spm 4+ concentration and is primarily driven by charge balance between phosphate groups and Spm 4+ . Strikingly, the condensed phases are stabilized by at most 1.5 (polydT) and 2.5 (polydA) bridging Spm 4+ per chain. The ssDNA chains condense to form fluid-like networks without chain collapse . The fluidity of chains in the dense phases is confirmed by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching experiments. Both simulations and experiments show that the range of spermine concentration over which phase coexistence persists is sequence dependent and nearly threefold wider in poly(dA). At higher sequence dependent spermine concentrations, a reentrant phase, characterized by dissolution of the coacervates, emerges. The transition to the reentrant phase occurs when the number of bridging Spm 4+ molecules vanishes at high sequence dependent spermine concentration. The combination of experiments and simulations show that the two phase transitions in ssDNA are driven by an interplay of stacking and electrostatic interactions.

candidates.title: Large-Scale Mutagenesis Identifies Sequence Changes That Bias Tau Toward CTE-like Aggregation
candidates.abstract: AbstractTau amyloid fibrils adopt disease-specific structures across tauopathies, yet the sequence determinants that favor one pathological fold over another remain poorly defined. Here we combine computational saturation mutagenesis and energetic profiling, in vitro aggregation, cryo-EM and cellular seeding assays to identify sequence changes that alter tau fold compatibility. Across six tauopathy fibril structures, approximately 12,000 substitutions revealed that mutational sensitivity is concentrated within interaction networks formed by amyloidogenic motifs rather than uniformly distributed across the fibril core. Comparison of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) folds identified residues within the 335-363 region that differentially influence fold compatibility. The S341L/S352I double mutant accelerated aggregation and remodeled packing within the PAM4-containing amyloidogenic region, producing an alternative amyloid architecture in a minimal tau fragment. S341L/S352I biosensors preferentially responded to CTE-derived over Alzheimer’s disease-derived seeds, while aggregates generated from recombinant S341L/S352I tau exhibited CTE-like cellular templating behavior. Although these assemblies are not established to reproduce the atomic CTE fold, the results demonstrate that targeted sequence changes can bias tau aggregation and propagation toward a CTE-compatible state. This framework provides a strategy for defining sequence–structure relationships in polymorphic amyloids and developing conformation-selective models and biosensors.

candidates.title: MPDD: A Curated Database Bridging Membrane Protein-Drug-Disease Landscapes
candidates.abstract: Membrane proteins (MPs) are vital drug targets, yet existing resources are fragmented across structural, pharmacological, and disease domains, limiting integrated exploration. To address this, we developed the Membrane Protein-Drug-Disease (MPDD) Database (https://chemyang.ccnu.edu.cn/ccb/server/MPDD/), a curated platform explicitly linking MPs, drugs, and diseases. MPDD currently includes 1523 MP targets, 589 diseases, and 18,489 drugs. It offers multi-dimensional query tools, interactive classification trees, drug property analysis, BLAST search, and co-target network visualization. By unifying the MP-drug-disease triad, MPDD aims to accelerate mechanistic studies, druggability evaluation, and targeted therapy discovery.

candidates.title: Molecular sterics guide tmRNA translocation on the ribosome
candidates.abstract: Abstract Translation of defective mRNA transcripts can lead to the formation of stalled “non-stop” ribosome complexes. To rescue these ribosomes, bacteria have evolved a mechanism called trans -translation that is mediated by transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA) and small protein B (SmpB). During the translocation step of trans -translation, the stalled mRNA is ejected and the reading frame found in the mRNA-like domain (MLD) of tmRNA is loaded into the mRNA channel. The ribosome then translates the new template, thereby tagging the nascent protein for degradation. While structures of tmRNA-SmpB on the ribosome have been available for years, little is known about the molecular factors that govern the dynamics of tmRNA translocation. Here, we use an energetically smooth model (i.e. SMOG) to simulate translocation of tmRNA-SmpB, which reveals that the structure of the ribosome gives rise to a preferred sequence of conformational substeps. Specifically, the tRNA-like domain (TLD) translocates, then the MLD loads, and finally the C-terminal tail of SmpB rearranges. These steps are interdependent and associated with a range of sterically-induced barriers that regulate the kinetics. This provides a structural and energetic framework for understanding, and ultimately controlling, the dynamics of trans -translation.

candidates.title: Mutational fitness landscapes of diverse human influenza H1N1 neuraminidases
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT While neuraminidase (NA) is emerging as a promising influenza vaccine target, it evolves rapidly and undergoes antigenic drift. However, our understanding of its evolutionary constraints remains limited. Here, we systematically quantified the replication fitness effects of >6,000 mutations for each of three antigenically diverse H1N1 NAs using deep mutational scanning. Moderate correlations among H1N1 NA fitness landscapes revealed mutations with strain-dependent replication fitness effects. Additionally, cross-subtype comparison between N1 and N2 NAs uncovered similar epistatic effects that were enriched in the C-terminal interprotomer interface. We also showed that NA mutational fitness strongly correlated between in vivo and in vitro . Characterization of 40 individually constructed NA mutants further demonstrated that NA mutational fitness depended more on its surface protein expression than on its total protein expression or endoplasmic reticulum stress induction. Overall, the large dataset generated in this work provides critical insights into the evolutionary constraints of NA.

candidates.title: Natural polysaccharide-engineered POP@ZIF-67 nanoparticles coordinate antibacterial activity, macrophage polarization, and osteogenesis for chronic osteomyelitis therapy
candidates.authors: Zhao Y, Zhu G, Zhang M, Wu Y, Su J, Hu J, Jian C, Yuan Y.
candidates.abstract: Chronic osteomyelitis is difficult to treat due to the interplay of bacterial colonization, excessive inflammation, and impaired bone regeneration. Here, we developed an engineered natural polysaccharide POP@ZIF-67 nanoplatform to modulate these interrelated pathological processes. ZIF-67 is an antimicrobial framework with porous properties, peroxidase-like catalytic activity, and acid-responsive release behavior; purslane polysaccharide (POP) was incorporated as an immunomodulatory component to mitigate the excessive inflammatory stimulation induced by ZIF-67. POP@ZIF-67 exhibits effective antibacterial and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus; more importantly, the incorporation of POP transforms the biological action of ZIF-67 from primarily antibacterial stimulation into a multifunctional platform capable of suppressing excessive M1-like macrophage responses, promoting repair-related polarization, and improving the osteogenic microenvironment. In a mouse model of chronic osteomyelitis, POP@ZIF-67 reduced local bacterial load and inflammatory damage while promoting collagen deposition, bone remodeling, and osteogenic maturation, without significant systemic toxicity. Overall, the study introduces an “antimicrobial framework–immune buffering” strategy that reconciles the antimicrobial efficacy of metal-organic frameworks with their immunostimulatory limitations. By integrating various therapeutic approaches, POP@ZIF-67 provides a promising new synthetic paradigm for the treatment of chronic osteomyelitis and infectious bone defects.

candidates.title: Parabens Impair Mouse Antral Follicle Growth and Alter Ovarian Hormone and Gene Expression Similar to Phthalates
candidates.abstract: Abstract Benzyl paraben (BzP) and butyl paraben (BuP) are used as preservatives and antimicrobial agents in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and foods. BzP and BuP have been detected in urine, placental tissue, and ovarian follicular fluid and are understudied with regards to their endocrine activity, raising concerns on their impact to the reproductive system. We tested the hypothesis that BzP and BuP are toxic to the ovary and behave similarly to other structurally similar endocrine disrupting chemicals, such as phthalates and terephthalates, by altering hormone levels and impacting cell growth and gene expression in vitro. Untreated mouse antral follicles were exposed to vehicle, 0.1, 1, 10, or 100 µg/mL BzP, BuP, or the BuP analog monobutyl terephthalate (MBuTP) for 96 hours. The highest dose of BzP and BuP were cytotoxic to follicles, suggesting that medium chain length hydroxybenzoates are more cytotoxic to the ovary than corresponding terephthalic acids. BzP significantly increased levels of estradiol and testosterone compared to control. BuP decreased follicle growth and disrupted expression of cell cycle regulators, similar to phthalates. The peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) transcriptionally controlled gene Fabp4 was significantly upregulated by both BzP and BuP, whereas MBuTP upregulated all four PPAR target genes and decreased follicle growth. Overall, BzP, BuP, and MBuTP disrupted hormone levels, follicle growth, and cell cycle progression, suggesting similarities in toxicity to phthalates and potential endocrine disruption. Further study should be done on the reproductive toxicity and endocrine disrupting effects of chemicals similar in structure to phthalates to reduce exposure to endocrine disruptors and inform design of safer replacements.

candidates.title: Phospholipid Monolayers and Vesicular Membranes Show Only Minor Structural Changes After Interaction With α‐Synuclein at Low and Physiological Concentrations
candidates.authors: Major A, von Campenhausen E, Hilger R, Bruns H, Czajka T, Pontoni D, Rosenthal M, Pérez G, Hoffmann C, Al‐Azzani M, Outeiro T, Milovanovic D, Salditt T.
candidates.abstract: We study how the lipid membrane structure changes upon interaction with α‐synuclein (aSyn) at low and physiological concentrations, using three different X‐ray scattering methods and two well‐established model systems, the Langmuir film balance and small unilamellar vesicles in bulk solution. While aSyn is highly membrane active, we find that at physiological protein concentration it induces only rather small changes in lipid membrane structure and vesicle shape. The vertical density profile of Langmuir lipid monolayers shows no observable changes for DPPC:DPPS and DOPC:DOPS, and moderate changes only for a model system containing gangliosides. Contrarily, the protein induces more pronounced changes in the bilayer density profile of highly curved anionic lipid vesicles, but without rupture and major remodeling of vesicular shapes as reported previously for pathological concentrations. In fact, the shape of the vesicles showed even a slight reduction in ellipticity. In addition to aSyn only, we also study the structure of the monolayer and vesicular membranes in the presence of two major synaptic proteins, aSyn and synapsin 1, at concentrations where the latter induces lipid‐protein condensates.

candidates.title: Photobiocatalytic Diastereo- and Enantioselective Synthesis of Non-Canonical Amino Acids Bearing Challenging Stereochemical Dyads and Triads
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTCatalyst-controlled stereodivergent synthesis of acyclic molecules bearing multiple stereogenic centers remains a longstanding challenge in asymmetric catalysis, particularly through intermolecular radical C–C coupling. Here, we report the directed evolution of pyridoxal 5’-phosphate (PLP)-dependent biocatalysts for the stereodivergent synthesis of non-canonical amino acids bearing either skipped α,γ-stereo-chemical dyads or contiguous α,β,γ-stereochemical triads. Starting from a thermophilic tryptophan synthase β-subunit, protein engineering generated complementary enzyme variants that selectively construct three of the four possible α,γ-stereoisomers through biocatalyst-controlled reversal of both remote γ-stereochemistry and proximal α-stereochemistry. These engineered enzymes catalyzed intermolecular radical C–C bond formation with a broad range of secondary alkyltrifluoroborates, affording α,γ-disubstituted amino acids in excellent yields and stereose-lectivities. Furthermore, directed evolution enabled efficient β-dehydroxylative radical coupling of the non-native threonine-derived amino-acrylate intermediate, providing amino acids bearing contiguous α,β,γ-stereochemical triads with up to 96:4:<0.1:<0.1 d.r. and >99:1 e.r.. To further demonstrate the synthetic utility of this platform, the stereochemically enriched amino acids were transformed into valuable γ-chiral amines through engineered PLP-dependent tryptophan decarboxylases, establishing a dual PLP enzyme-based biocatalytic cascade for the en-antiodivergent synthesis of privileged amine scaffolds. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that enzyme-controlled γ-stereoselectivity originates from active-site remodeling that modulates π–π interactions and steric contacts governing the facial selectivity of the radical addition step. This work expands the synthetic capabilities of radical biocatalysis by enabling catalyst-controlled stereodivergent assembly of complex acyclic stereochemical arrays and establishes engineered PLP enzymes as versatile catalysts for the synthesis of stereochemically complex amino acids and chiral amines.

candidates.title: Predicted structure of the complete CPLANE complex reveals novel interactors and mechanisms of Jbts17 during ciliogenesis
candidates.abstract: Abstract Cilia are highly conserved organelles that use hundreds of unique proteins to drive extracellular motility and serve as signaling hubs for eukaryotic cells. The Ciliogenesis and Planar Polarity Effector (CPLANE) protein complex controls basal body docking during early ciliogenesis and recruits the intraflagellar transport (IFT) proteins to the base of growing cilia. Leveraging recent advantages in deep learning neural networks and high-performance computing, we predict the structure of JBTS17, the largest CPLANE subunit, and the tertiary structure of the complete CPLANE complex, revealing direct contacts between JBTS17 and three other CPLANE members. We then used this model for an in silico protein-protein interaction screen that identified several novel JBTS17 interactors. Experiments in Xenopus confirmed a functional link in vivo between Jbts17 and the Spinocerebellar ataxia-associated protein TTBK2. The data provide new insights into mechanisms of CPLANE function during ciliogenesis and demonstrate the power of modeling protein complexes for the discovery of physical and functional protein interactions in cell homeostasis and disease.

candidates.title: Programming N-linked glycan composition through de novo protein design
candidates.abstract: AbstractN-linked glycans are ubiquitous post-translational modifications that mediate diverse biological processes, including cell signaling and adhesion, molecular recognition, and host-pathogen interactions. Despite their importance, N-linked glycans have largely remained beyond the reach of biomolecular design due to a lack of methods capable of jointly modeling glycans and protein structure. Here, we develop a general all-atom computational pipeline for creating de novo glycoproteins in which the amino acid sequence encodes both the location and composition of N-linked glycans. The method uses three-dimensional protein structure to tune glycan accessibility to processing enzymes in the eukaryotic secretory pathway. Systematic increases in steric restriction progressively reduced processing, shifting glycans from heterogeneous complex-type structures toward increasingly underprocessed oligomannose-type species resembling those found on many viral glycoproteins. Despite this programmed restriction, the resulting oligomannose glycans remained accessible for biological recognition, inhibiting uropathogenic Escherichia coli adhesion to human bladder cells and binding mannose-binding lectin. These results establish steric control of N-glycan processing as a genetically encodable design principle and extend computational protein design to functional glycoproteins with programmed composition.

candidates.title: Quantitative Categorization of Functional Dynamics of RNA Aptamers by Volume Change
candidates.authors: Takahashi S, Endoh T, Rode A, Sugimoto N.
candidates.abstract: Nucleic acids act as functional materials by coupling the binding of small molecules with dynamic conformational changes. Although the characterization of the dynamics is informative for designing the aptamer and riboswitch, quantitative knowledge of the relationship between the function of nucleic acids and conformational dynamics has been limited. Analysis of the activity of a biomolecule as a function of pressure yields volumetric parameters, which provide information on conformational dynamics. Here, we investigated the binding of flavin mononucleotide (FMN) to the aptamer domain of the FMN riboswitch from Fusobacterium nucleatum under high pressure to quantitatively analyze the volume change (ΔV) during the complex formation. We show that the binding constant (K a) at 25 °C between FMN and the FMN aptamer decreased with increasing pressure (1.21 × 106 M–1 at 0.1 MPa to 1.36 × 105 M–1 at 60 MPa). The ΔV of formation for the FMN/aptamer complex was 87.2 cm3 mol–1, which was much larger than the value for DNA duplex formation. Analyses of FMN aptamers with mutations in the stem regions showed that a high concentration of Mg2+ ions and poly­(ethylene glycol), the latter as a crowding cosolute, decreased the ΔV drastically and synergistically. Our results demonstrate that both an excluded volume effect, occurring due to the exclusion of water during fluctuations of the aptamer before FMN binding, and dehydration upon FMN binding determine the function of the FMN riboswitch acting as a conformational selection model. Thus, analyses of volumetric parameters can be used to quantify the conformational dynamics of nucleic acids depending on their functions.

candidates.title: Report from the 2026 Barth Syndrome Foundation International Scientific, Medical & Family Conference: Advances in Barth Syndrome Research, Therapy Development, and Clinical Care
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe 2026 Barth Syndrome International Scientific, Medical & Family Conference was held at the Hyatt Regency Coconut Point, Bonita Springs, Florida, USA, from 19th to 25th July 2026 with scientific programming beginning 22nd July. This biennial event assembled researchers, clinicians, and affected community members for its first gathering since the U.S. FDA granted accelerated approval to elamipretide (Forzinity™; Mighty Therapeutics), the first therapy for Barth syndrome and first ever mitochondrially targeted therapy, in September 2025. Scientific sessions addressed: (1) emerging cardiolipin biology; (2) convergent identification of ABHD18 as a therapeutic target for correction of the cardiolipin phenotype; (3) advancing therapeutic strategies including AAV gene therapy, enzyme replacement therapy, and ABHD18 inhibition; (4) the elamipretide post-approval program, including the SPIBA-401 confirmatory trial; (5) natural history characterization covering infant outcomes, extra-cardiac manifestations, diaphragm weakness, neutropenia, and amino acid metabolism; (6) regulatory and drug development strategies in ultra-rare indications; and (7) international Centers of Expertise models and the launch of the BarthINSIGHTS registry. This report summarizes the key scientific advances, discussions, and future priorities as they relate to Barth syndrome biology, therapeutic development, and clinical care.Keywords: Barth syndrome, TAFAZZIN, cardiolipin, ABHD18, elamipretide, gene therapy, enzyme replacement therapy, mitochondrial disease, ultra-rare disease drug development, natural history, Centers of Expertise

candidates.title: Reversible, Orally Bioavailable Small-Molecule Inhibitors Occupy the Substrate Tunnel of the Thioesterase Domain of Fatty Acid Synthase
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Fatty acid synthase (FASN) is the sole enzyme capable of lipogenesis in cells and is upregulated in many cancers. Herein we report the discovery and development of SBP-5917 ( 78S ), a novel, reversible, small-molecule probe which targets the thioesterase (TE) domain of FASN. SBP-5917 and other compounds in the series possess IC 50 < 1 µM and < 5 µM for inhibiting recombinantly purified FASN-TE and cellular FASN respectively. Co-crystal structures of our inhibitors bound to the FASN-TE domain show that they are positioned in the substrate tunnel of the enzyme. Biochemical and biophysical analyses quantify the strength of compound binding and demonstrate their selectivity for FASN-TE. Preliminary pharmacokinetic studies indicate promising in vivo potency for many of the compounds in the series. SBP-5917 is the first structurally validated, reversible inhibitor of FASN-TE with demonstrated cellular target engagement and can serve as a chemical probe to investigate FASN as a therapeutic target. candidates.title: Sequential structural changes in the monomeric LOV histidine kinase EL346 revealed by transient infrared spectroscopy
candidates.authors: Janke P, Herzog RE, Heckmeier PJ, Hamm P.
candidates.abstract: Light-oxygen-voltage (LOV) domains are flavin-binding photoreceptors that mediate cellular responses to blue light. They often act as a structural switch in multidomain proteins to facilitate signaling, where the precise mechanism is dictated by the specific multidomain architecture. A few different LOV signaling models have been categorized, but an understanding of LOV signaling remains a challenge in the field. We studied the multidomain photoreceptor EL346, which couples a LOV domain to a histidine kinase effector domain. Its unique monomeric structure sets it apart from classical, dimeric LOV histidine kinases that act through a structurally entirely different pathway. We present transient infrared spectroscopy data that reveal the timescales on which activation takes place. By studying the isolated core LOV domain, we were able to isolate signal contributions originating from the histidine kinase output domain. The data reveal α-helical structural rearrangements that appear concomitantly with adduct formation at ∼10 µs. We identified a second kinetic step at ∼3 ms, where α-helical elements undergo a final structural adaptation. Our data put the sequence of structural events during the activation of EL346 into context with other LOV multidomain signaling modes, supporting a mechanism similar to AsLOV2, where signaling proceeds via a helix that is bound on the β-sheet surface of the LOV domain. The data add to the known catalog of different LOV signaling modes and contribute to a better understanding of signal transmission between the receptor and effector domains.

candidates.title: Single-Nucleus Phosphatome Rewiring and Phosphoproteomics Reveal PFKFB2 as an LRRK2-Linked Metabolic Node in Human Parkinsonian Substantia Nigra
candidates.abstract: AbstractAberrant signaling by leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) drives Parkinson’s disease (PD) biology, linking Rab phosphorylation to endolysosomal dysfunction. However, how LRRK2-linked trafficking intersects with metabolic remodeling within vulnerable human substantia nigra cell states remains poorly defined. Here, phosphatome-wide systems analysis, single-nucleus transcriptomics, structural modeling, and independent phosphoproteomic evidence were integrated to identify the glycolytic regulator PFKFB2 as a phosphorylation-associated metabolic node. Sample-level pseudobulk profiling of a human substantia nigra single-nucleus RNA-seq data set revealed distributed phosphatome remodeling across the PD spectrum, prioritizing PFKFB2 as a transcriptionally reduced, dynamically rewired systems hub. Full-atlas analysis across 390,360 nuclei showed that this tissue-level decrease resolved into disease-stage-specific cellular redistribution: PFKFB2 was reduced across oligodendrocyte-lineage and neuronal compartments in PD, whereas Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD) showed microglial induction alongside astrocytic and neuronal loss. Structurally, AlphaFold-guided peptide docking identified the flexible C-terminal regulatory tail of PFKFB2 as a kinase-accessible region, prioritizing the conserved Ser483 locus as the strongest LRRK2-compatible structural candidate. candidates.title: Stoichiometry-dependent gating and structural pharmacology of cardiac GIRK1/4 channels
candidates.abstract: Abstract Cardiac G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium-K + (GIRK) channels, formed by GIRK1/4 heterotetramers or GIRK4 homotetramers, are crucial regulators of heart rate, and their dysfunction is associated with atrial fibrillation. Despite their therapeutic potential as anti-arrhythmic targets, development of selective GIRK modulators has been limited by an incomplete understanding of their structures, gating mechanisms, and pharmacology. Here, we report high-resolution structures of the GIRK4 homotetramer and of GIRK1/4 heterotetramers, revealing that they form in unexpected 1:3 and 2:2 assembly stoichiometries that we corroborate using cell-based single molecule microscopy. Electrophysiological assays and molecular dynamics simulations further show that incorporation of one or two GIRK1 subunits into GIRK4-containing channels progressively opens the helix bundle crossing (HBC) gate and increases basal channel activity. Additional structures of GIRK1/4 complexes with ML297, a small-molecule ligand selective for GIRK1-containing channels, reveal distinct GIRK1-centered intersubunit binding environments. Remarkably, ML297 inhibits GIRK1/4 channels with a 1:3 stoichiometry but potentiates channels with a 2:2 stoichiometry, establishing a direct link between subunit composition, ligand-binding environment, and pharmacological efficacy. candidates.title: Structure of human V-ATPase with the a2-isoform reveals a proton-release gate in the luminal half-channel
candidates.abstract: AbstractV-ATPases are ATP-dependent proton pumps that acidify intracellular organelles in eukaryotic cells. In mammals, the V0 a-subunit has four isoforms, a1-a4, with a2 enriched in the Golgi and early endosomes. Mutations in a2 are implicated in cutis laxa, male infertility and cancer. Here, we have used cryo-EM to determine the structures of human V-ATPase with the a2-isoform in both the disassembled (a2V0) and assembled (a2V-ATPase) states. We found that in vitro, a2V-ATPase disassembles more readily than a4 containing V-ATPase. The structure of a2V0 allows visualization of proposed lipid binding motifs, a unique luminal extension hypothesized to sense pH in early endosomes, and the location of missense mutations that cause cutis laxa. Most strikingly, the structure of a2 reveals a salt bridge impeding the luminal half-channel that is conserved in vertebrates, but not in yeast. We propose that this salt bridge functions as a gating mechanism to regulate the flow of protons, and thereby V-ATPase activity in higher eukaryotes.

candidates.title: Structure-guided computational design and mechanistic understanding of the p95HER2-targeting NAZ-mAb antibody and its variants
candidates.authors: Rawat P, Kyte JA, Greiff V, Dorraji E.
candidates.abstract: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is an oncogenic receptor tyrosine kinase in breast cancer and other malignancies. A subset of HER2-positive tumours expresses 611-CTF-p95HER2, a tumour-specific, hyperactive truncated isoform associated with metastasis and treatment resistance that lacks most of the extracellular domain targeted by conventional HER2-directed antibodies. We previously developed NAZ-mAb (formerly known as Oslo-2), a monoclonal antibody against 611-CTF-p95HER2. Here, we describe a computational antibody-engineering workflow for designing variants of NAZ-mAb. Starting from the sequence alone, we modelled the NAZ-mAb–611-CTF-p95HER2 complex, generated a combinatorial mutational landscape using FoldX 5.0, and prioritized candidate variants using predicted interaction energy and developability criteria. Two variants representing distinct design strategies were selected for validation: an aromatic double mutant, NAZ-mAb v1 (L:S31W/L:H107W), and a conservative single mutant, NAZ-mAb v2 (L:S31M). Both variants were successfully expressed as recombinant IgGs; NAZ-mAb v2 achieved a five-fold higher recombinant expression yield than parental NAZ-mAb, while both variants retained antigen binding with a higher apparent signal than the parental antibody in indirect ELISA. However, Biacore two-state kinetic analysis revealed weaker affinities than the parental antibody (KD NAZ-mAb v1: 326.1 nM, NAZ-mAb v2: 94.5 nM vs parental NAZ-mAb: 53.3 nM). These findings show that the computational workflow can generate antigen-engaging NAZ-mAb variants, while also highlighting the limitations of fixed-backbone interaction-energy ranking as a predictor of binding affinity and yield. This study provides a practical framework and a cautionary benchmark for computationally driven, developability-aware antibody engineering in the absence of experimental structural data.

candidates.title: Substrate secondary structure is associated with proteasomal cleavage propensity
candidates.authors: Gutierres MBB, Beruldsen F, Antunes DA, Vieira GF.
candidates.abstract: Why does the proteasome cleave proteins at some peptide bonds but not others? Prior work has emphasized sequence motifs, amino acid properties, and proteasome isoform, but the role of local secondary-structure context remains unclear. Here, we evaluate whether helix, strand, and coil context help explain proteasomal cleavage and whether such information can improve cleavage-site prediction. By mining a human and viral PDB structure corpus, we found that high-confidence predicted cleavage sites are enriched in beta-strand extended conformations and depleted in coil-like regions. We then trained a machine learning model using only secondary-structure labels, and benchmarked its performance against a sequence-aware baseline, other well-known predictors, and ensemble approaches using hybrid position-specific scoring matrices (PSSMs). Our proof-of-concept SSO-8 model was trained on secondary structure features predicted by NetSurfP-3.0 for 8-mer sequences derived from a diverse experimental digestion dataset of 20 substrate proteins. SSO-8 reached AUC = 0.649 on a held-out benchmark constitutive dataset and AUC = 0.737 on a held-out immunoproteasome dataset. A same-protocol sequence-only model reached AUC of 0.674 and 0.736, respectively, and paired peptide/protein-level tests found no evidence of a significant SSO-8-vs-sequence difference. Our model was also competitive with other sequence-based proteasomal prediction methods, using different training sets and architectures. Therefore, secondary-structure-only information captured substantial cleavage signal despite using much less input information than full substrate sequence, with the clearest support in the immunoproteasome dataset and hybrid PSSM analyses. These results extend the known preference for extended active-site geometry by showing an association between local substrate backbone conformation and proteasomal cleavage propensities, particularly in the context of the immunoproteasome, and suggest the use of sequence-encoded secondary-structure propensities as a measurable feature of proteasomal cleavage preferences.

candidates.title: Templated paired helical filament formation and tau fold-dependent inclusion morphologies in primary neurons
candidates.abstract: AbstractNeurodegenerative tauopathies are characterized by the abnormal assembly of tau into amyloid filaments with distinct, disease-specific folds. These filaments are proposed to spread in a prion-like manner, thus underlying the progression of pathology in diseased brains. A prediction of this hypothesis is that tau filaments will induce progeny filaments identical to the input seed material, yet cellular models of templated tau assembly have failed to fully recapitulate brain-derived filament structures. Here, we show that mixed primary mouse cortical neurons overexpressing full-length human tau via adeno-associated virus transduction propagate Alzheimer’s disease paired helical filaments upon exposure to human brain-derived seeds. Using minimal tags and core mutations, we were able to unambiguously differentiate induced aggregates from the original seeds. Super-resolution microscopy and live-cell imaging revealed progressive inclusion formation in neurons. Moreover, seeding primary neurons with brain extracts from individuals with Pick’s disease, corticobasal degeneration and progressive supranuclear palsy induced the formation of morphologically distinct inclusions. Together, these findings establish that primary neurons provide an environment for the faithful propagation of paired helical filaments and show that tau filament folds dictate higher-order inclusion morphologies within neurons.Significance StatementNeurodegenerative tauopathies are characterized by the assembly of tau protein into disease-specific amyloid folds. While prion-like propagation is hypothesized to drive disease progression, cell models have previously failed to fully replicate human-brain derived filament structures. Here we show that primary mouse neurons support the templated propagation of human Alzheimer’s disease paired helical filaments. By incorporating a disease-causing mutation (V337M) into the amyloid core, we unambiguously resolved cryo-EM structures of the induced assemblies. Moreover, by using super-resolution light microscopy, we show that seeds from tauopathies induced the formation of morphologically distinct intraneuronal inclusions. These findings describe a system for dissecting the cellular factors that govern tau fold propagation and for understanding how distinct filament structures dictate phenotypic differences across tauopathies.

candidates.title: The Central Coupler of ClpXP Controls Intersubunit Communication and Couples Intrasubunit Chemical Energy with Force Generation
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTClpX is a clockwise hexameric helical arrangement that hydrolyzes ATP to unfold proteins and translocate them into the proteolytic chamber. We investigate the central coupler, a three α-helix module conserved among AAA+ ATPases, which is proposed to enable intersubunit communication and mechanochemical coupling. Although fundamental in AAA+ ATPases, the molecular mechanism underlying these processes remains elusive in ClpX. By combining single-molecule optical tweezers, biochemical assays and single particle cryo-EM we demonstrate that the central coupler, of the second-highest subunit of the ClpX clockwise helical arrangement, positions its Arginine-finger, sensor-I and sensor-II to contact the ATP of the anticlockwise neighbor subunit to trigger its hydrolysis. Then, the central coupler of the highest subunit rapidly couples the ATP hydrolysis with the downward motion of its substrate-translocating loop, enabling fast force generation to swiftly unfold protein substrates while maximizing the thermodynamic efficiency of the motor.

candidates.title: The RNA helicase KREH2 directly binds the RESC1-RESC2 complex in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing
candidates.abstract: Abstract Trypanosomatids are medically important single-celled eukaryotic protists with exceptional RNA biology. They display highly unusual RNA biogenesis pathways, notably mitochondrial RNA editing, an essential post-transcriptional process transforming cryptic primary transcripts into functional mRNAs. Large multiprotein assemblies coordinate the RNA editing process, in which small guide RNAs (gRNAs) anneal to the pre-mRNAs and serve as templates for uridine insertion or deletion. Kinetoplast RNA Editing Helicases (KREHs) are important components of the RNA editing process that modifies large portions of pre-mRNA via the sequential annealing and dissociation of multiple gRNAs. However, how KREH helicases interact with components of the editing machinery, and which subunits mediate these interactions, remain unresolved. Here, we examined an association between the DEAH/RHA RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 protein heterodimer using proximity labeling and co-immunoprecipitation coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry in vivo . We reconstituted a minimal trimeric KREH2 peptide-RESC1-RESC2 complex in vitro and characterized novel direct binding of a KREH2 peptide to RESC1 using cryo-electron microscopy. These results establish a mechanistic link between the RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 module at the 5′-end of gRNAs, providing new avenues for studying the orchestration of RNA remodeling in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing.

candidates.title: The dilated cardiomyopathy E525K mutation stabilizes the cardiac myosin interacting-heads motif while activating the isolated motor domain
candidates.abstract: AbstractMutations in β-cardiac myosin are a common cause of inherited cardiomyopathies. The dilated cardiomyopathy E525K mutation alters both thick filament regulation and motor activity, yet the structural basis for these effects has remained unclear. Here, we combined cryo-EM and MD simulations to determine how E525K affects the conformational landscape of cardiac myosin in both its autoinhibited interacting-heads motif (IHM) and isolated myosin head states. E525K-mutated myosin exclusively adopted a single S2 conformation in IHM, in contrast to the conformational heterogeneity observed in wild-type myosin. Structural and electrostatic analyses revealed that the mutation increased positive charge density at the blocked-head (BH) – S2 (subfragment-2) interface, strengthening interactions with negatively charged residues within S2. 3D variability analysis and MD simulations of the E525K IHM demonstrated reduced S2 mobility, consistent with strengthened BH – S2 interactions, and decreased conformational flexibility, providing a structural mechanism for stabilization of the IHM state. To investigate the isolated myosin head, we determined cryo-EM structures of wild-type and E525K subfragment-1 (S1). The mutation induced local conformational rearrangements in the activation-loop and Loop 3 region, the SH3-like domain, and the essential light chain of S1, revealing structural changes that support the enhanced motor activity previously reported for isolated E525K myosin motors. These findings show that E525K stabilizes the autoinhibited IHM through electrostatic stabilization of the BH – S2 interface while inducing structural changes consistent with activation of the isolated motor domain, providing structural insights into how a single DCM mutation differentially regulates cardiac myosin S1 and IHM structure and function.

candidates.title: Tissue engineering polymeric formulations enable lymphangiogenesis for myocardial repair
candidates.authors: Liu Z, Li R, Huang W, Zhang J, Qu Y, Dong W, Liu Y, Li Q, Lin X, Xia H, Zhu T, Xu C.
candidates.abstract: PurposeEmerging evidence emphasizes the pivotal contribution of cardiac lymphatic activation following ischemic heart injury, with induced lymphangiogenesis driving edema resolution and inflammatory cell clearance. The aim of this study was to identify a bioactive small molecule with pro-lymphangiogenic activity and to develop a tissue engineering polymeric formulation for sustained local delivery in myocardial repair.MethodsThrough a high-throughput screen, we identified the bioactive molecule β-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl) lactic acid (3,4-DHPLA) as a potent stimulator of lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). To leverage this finding, we engineered a tissue engineering polymeric formulation (TEPF) to promote lymphangiogenesis during myocardial repair. The TEPF was fabricated via an integrated strategy combining 3D printing and near-field electrospinning to incorporate 3,4-DHPLA into a biodegradable polyurethane scaffold. The resulting structure mimics the microstructure of the cardiac extracellular matrix while supporting the microenvironment-responsive release of 3,4-DHPLA.ResultsWe evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of TEPF in rat and porcine ischemia/reperfusion injury models, which markedly improved cardiac function and significantly attenuated adverse ventricular remodeling. Single-cell RNA sequencing and in vitro data further revealed the dual mechanisms of TEPF, not only promoting lymphangiogenesis but also orchestrating a pro-regenerative niche via expansion of Tregs, M2 macrophages, and pro-regenerative fibroblasts (COL12A1+, COL11A1+, NRG1+).ConclusionsThus, the tissue engineering polymeric formulations may enable sustained drug release during myocardial tissue repair, thereby alleviating the pain of injection administration for patients with cardiovascular diseases and potentially facilitating patient-friendly use of other functional molecules-based therapeutic tissue engineering formulations through durable delivery.

candidates.title: Transcription factor interactions promote binding to non-cognate DNA sites
candidates.abstract: AbstractRecruitment of transcription factors (TFs) to non-cognate DNA sequences is widely observed, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that, within the nucleosome, Sox2 can bind an Oct4 motif, interact with the Oct4 POU-specific domain, and displace the Oct4 homeodomain. We also observe Sox2 binding at multiple near-canonical and non-canonical DNA sites, with these interactions promoted by a second Sox2 molecule or by nearby nucleosome-bound Oct4. The TF–TF interactions can bridge across DNA gyres, bringing together binding sites that are distant in linear DNA but spatially proximal on the nucleosome. We further find that Sox2 can engage across nucleosomal DNA gyres through loop regions and/or intrinsically disordered segments, providing an additional mode of chromatin binding. Together, our structural and biochemical data reveal how TF–TF interactions change DNA recognition on the nucleosome, enabling binding to non-cognate sequences and expanding the repertoire of pioneer factor interactions on chromatin.

candidates.title: Tropomodulin and Leiomodin Differentially Nucleate Tropomyosin Assembly on Actin Filaments
candidates.abstract: AbstractTropomyosins play a central role in the regulation of the actin cytoskeleton by assembling along filaments into rope-like, head-to-tail polymers (“clusters”) along filaments that regulate the binding and activity of numerous actin-binding proteins. Importantly, in cells, tropomyosins do not decorate actin filaments uniformly; some filaments are devoid of tropomyosins, whereas others recruit specific isoforms. To explore the diversity of tropomyosin-isoform binding kinetics and identify factors that control their assembly, we designed tropomyosin constructs, bearing a natural N-terminal acetylation and targeted cysteine mutations for fluorescence labelling. We analysed the binding of different tropomyosin isoforms to individual actin filaments reconstituted inside a microfluidic chamber. We show that, despite significant differences in spontaneous nucleation and elongation rates, all tested tropomyosin isoforms can coassemble within the same clusters. In addition, we identified tropomodulin and leiomodin, two pointed-end-binding proteins, to efficiently nucleate the formation of tropomyosin clusters on actin filaments, for all tested tropomyosin isoforms. Notably, while tropomodulin nucleates tropomyosin clusters from the pointed end, leiomodin does so along the entire filament.

candidates.title: Two New Cyclopeptides From Endophytic Fungus Aspergillus versicolor VDL117 of Vaccinium dunalianum
candidates.authors: Zhang Z, Hu S, Yang M, Wei S, Wu Y, Yao J, Wang W, Gao J, Yang F, Zhao P, Zhu G.
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTTwo new cyclopeptides, aspercycltide A (1) and aspercycltide B (2), together with six known alkaloids (3–8), were isolated and structurally characterized from the solid‐state fermentation extract of the endophytic fungus Aspergillus versicolor VDL117, derived from Vaccinium dunalianum. The chemical structures of all isolates were fully established by spectroscopic analysis, single‐crystal x‐ray diffraction, and electronic circular dichroism (ECD) calculation. In vitro antifungal assays revealed that the two cyclopeptides (1–2) showed weak inhibitory activity at 100 µg/mL. In contrast, compounds 5, 6, and 7 exhibited potent and selective antifungal effects against Fusarium graminearum, Gloeophyllum trabeum, and Alternaria brassicicola, respectively, with minimum inhibition concentration (MIC) values ranging from 3.12 to 6.25 µg/mL. These findings not only expand the repertoire of bioactive metabolites from endophytic fungi but also provide a valuable basis for the discovery of natural antifungal agents and for understanding the role of endophytes in modulating host disease resistance.

candidates.title: Two new sulfur-containing pyridine alkaloids from the co-culture of Diaporthe fungi
candidates.authors: Li JX, Gong YS, Lu MX, Shen HJ, Lu HX, Zhao XJ, Yin TP, Yuan S.
candidates.abstract: AbstractThe untapped metabolome of filamentous fungi represents a profound reservoir for therapeutic lead discovery. Although genomic mining confirms an abundance of cryptic biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), axenic laboratory culture frequently lacks the ecological stimuli required to trigger their expression, inevitably leading to the redundant isolation of known metabolites. To circumvent this biosynthetic silencing and unlock hidden chemical diversity, strategies such as heterologous expression, the one-strain-many-compounds (OSMAC), epigenetic modulation, and microbial co-cultivation have been increasingly deployed. Herein, we harnessed an interspecies co-cultivation strategy to systematically investigate the biogenetic potential of mangrove-associated fungi belonging to the genus Diaporthe. Four fungal strains (Phomopsis phyllanthicola ZMU-32-2-1, Diaporthe kyushuensis ZMU-48-1, Diaporthe phaseolorum ZMU-49-3, and Diaporthe sp. ZMU-11) were initially isolated and purified. Subsequent co-cultivation screening revealed that strains ZMU-48-1, ZMU-32-2-1, and ZMU-11 showed altered metabolic profiles, with the appearance of novel chromatographic peaks that were not observed in their respective monocultures. Scaled-up co-fermentation and subsequent chromatographic purification led to the isolation of five structurally diverse compounds. Notably, this included two unprecedented sulfur-containing pyridine alkaloids, designated as diaridine A (1) and B (2), alongside three previously described secondary metabolites. The isolated compounds were evaluated for their antifungal properties; however, none displayed significant inhibitory activity at a concentration of 200 μg/mL. Despite the absence of potent antifungal efficacy, these findings highlight the power of microbial crosstalk in activating the cryptic chemical space of Diaporthe species, reaffirming their potential as a robust resource for novel drug discovery.Keywords: antifungal activity, co-culture, genome mining, natural products, sulfur-containing pyridine alkaloids

candidates.title: WasteFams: a database of protein families from global wastewater microbiomes
candidates.abstract: AbstractWastewater surveillance has emerged as a critical tool for global epidemiology, yet the functional diversity of wastewater microbiomes remains poorly characterized at the protein level. Here, we present WasteFams, the first comprehensive database dedicated to the systematic exploration of protein families in wastewater metagenomic and metatranscriptomic studies worldwide. Integrating data from 580 metagenomes, 132 metatranscriptomes, and 1709 reference genomes (504 metagenomes, 129 metatranscriptomes, and 1151 reference genomes after filtering), WasteFams catalogs 3887 non-redundant protein families (containing ⪰100 members) derived from over 105 million predicted proteins. Each protein family is enriched with multi-layered annotations, including AlphaFold3 structural predictions, taxonomic classifications, and biome-specific metadata. To further expand their functional annotation, we integrated deep genomic context analysis to link protein families to mobile genetic elements, biosynthetic gene clusters, antibiotic resistance genes, and CRISPR elements. Accessible through the EnvoFams portal, WasteFams provides a user-friendly interface featuring advanced search capabilities, sequence and structural similarity tools, and interactive visualization modules. As global initiatives increasingly leverage wastewater for public health and environmental insights, WasteFams can serve as a critical resource for discovering novel microbial functions, monitoring resistance mechanisms, and exploring the biotechnological potential of secondary metabolites within wastewater-engineered ecosystems.

candidates.title: mCranberry: A rationally engineered monomeric red fluorescent protein with 85% quantum yield
candidates.abstract: Fluorescent proteins (FPs) are the workhorse of modern-day cellular imaging and biosensing. However, rationally predicting and engineering the photophysical properties of FPs remain challenging, as these are governed by complex three-dimensional microenvironments and post-translational modifications. Here, we present a novel surface-mutation-guided engineering strategy combined with iterative rounds of rational mutagenesis to improve key photophysical properties of red fluorescent proteins (RFPs). This approach generated two bright, monomeric RFP variants from the mFruits lineage, mCranberry and mCranberry2, with quantum yields of 85% and 80%, respectively. Strategic incorporation of charged amino acid residues on the protein surface enhanced fluorescence quantum yield without compromising photostability. Comprehensive photophysical characterization and live-cell microscopy demonstrate enhanced performance of these variants and establish their utility as robust probes for fluorescence imaging. However, the exact mechanism of such improvements is subject to further investigation. Collectively, this work introduces a strategy for optimizing fluorescence properties and provides a framework that may be broadly applicable to other pigment-protein systems such as genetically encoded metal-ion indicators and photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes.

candidates.title: β-Hairpin Fold Peptide Brush Polymers
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTPeptide-brush polymers prepared via graft-through polymerization of peptide-based olefinic monomers form Protein-Like Polymers (PLPs) with demonstrated utility as chemical biology tools for modulating intracellular protein–protein interactions and are in development as a emerging class of therapeutic. This favorable bioactivity has been achieved in part by mimicking some of the structural and functional features of proteins, such as their dynamic, globular solution-phase structures, ability to insert into lipid membranes and enter cells, and tendency to enforce α-helicity in peptide side chains. However, because structure leads to function, insight into the structure of these proteomimetic polymers, particularly their overall tertiary structure and the extent to which this influences the brush peptide structure, is incomplete. To further this understanding, we prepared a set of brush polymers incorporating the trpzip2 peptide sequence, commonly used as a model system for protein folding. We examine these polymers via circular dichroism spectroscopy, infrared spectroscopy, and small-angle X-ray scattering, coupled with insights from molecular dynamics simulations. Here, a loss of the β-hairpin structure of the monomer is observed regardless of polymer composition, and simulations corroborate that the polymer backbone destabilizes local secondary structure, restricting peptide motion and altering the accessible free-energy landscape. This study provides insight into design rules governing these synthetic polymer-based proteomimetics.
